1.name: Ar-Rahman
1.meaning: The Most Merciful, whose mercy embraces all that exists.
1.description:
Ar-Rahman comes from the Arabic root r-h-m, which carries the sense of mercy, tenderness and protection. The word for the womb, rahim, shares this root. Just as the womb shelters and nourishes a life without asking anything in return, this name speaks of a mercy that is vast, unearned and all-encompassing.

The fa'lan pattern of the word conveys fullness, a mercy that overflows and fills everything. It reaches believer and unbeliever, human, animal and plant alike: every breath, every sunrise and every rainfall is a sign of it. For this reason, Ar-Rahman is used for Allah alone; no created being is ever called by this name.

In the Qur'an, Ar-Rahman appears in the basmala that opens every surah except At-Tawbah, and an entire surah bears its name. Surah Ar-Rahman opens with it and lists teaching the Qur'an, creating the human being and granting the gift of speech among the first expressions of this mercy. In Al-Isra, believers are told they may call upon Him as Allah or as Ar-Rahman, showing how closely the two names are held together.

verses.text: The Most Merciful Taught the Qur'an, Created man, [And] taught him eloquence.

1.reflection: The first breath you took this morning was not something you earned; it was given to you freely. Ar-Rahman reminds you that goodness reached you long before anything was asked of you. Try looking at what you have today as a gift rather than a given. You may find it easier, then, to be kind to others without keeping score.
1.practice: Do a small kindness today for someone who expects nothing from you, and expect nothing in return.

2.name: Ar-Rahim
2.meaning: The Especially Merciful, whose mercy is constant and personal.
2.description:
Ar-Rahim shares the root r-h-m with Ar-Rahman and likewise speaks of mercy and compassion. Its fa'il pattern, however, highlights continuity and depth. If Ar-Rahman describes how wide mercy reaches, Ar-Rahim describes how it keeps coming, steady and close.

Scholars often explain the two names side by side: Ar-Rahman is the mercy that embraces all creation in this world, while Ar-Rahim is the special, lasting mercy shown to those who believe, turn to Him and ask for help. The Qur'an also uses the word rahim for the Prophet (At-Tawbah 9:128), a reminder that mercy is a quality human beings can reflect as well.

In the Qur'an, Ar-Rahim appears alongside Ar-Rahman in the basmala and is frequently paired with Al-Ghafur (the Forgiving) and Ar-Ra'uf (the Kind). These pairings point to forgiveness and gentleness as expressions of His mercy.

verses.text: And your god is one God. There is no deity [worthy of worship] except Him, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

2.reflection: Mercy is not a single act that runs out; it is a posture you return to again and again. Ar-Rahim reminds you that the mercy shown to you has never worn thin. Today you can be gentle one more time, with someone who got it wrong or with yourself. Sometimes mercy is not a grand sacrifice, just a softer tone of voice.
2.practice: Send a kind message today to someone who wronged you, without reopening the issue.

3.name: Al-Malik
3.meaning: The Sovereign, the true King and Owner of all.
3.description:
Al-Malik comes from the root m-l-k, which means to own, to govern and to rule. The words mulk (dominion, possession) and mamlaka (kingdom) share this root. Al-Malik is the One who holds authority, who commands and forbids.

Human ownership and power are temporary, limited and entrusted. Allah's sovereignty was taken from no one, depends on no one and has no end. This name is a reminder that true ownership belongs to Him alone, and that whatever is in human hands has only been placed there for a while.

The name Al-Malik appears in Ta-Ha 20:114, Al-Mu'minun 23:116, Al-Hashr 59:23 and Al-Jumu'ah 62:1, and in Surah An-Nas He is called the King of mankind. In these verses Al-Malik is often joined with Al-Haqq (the Truth) and Al-Quddus (the Pure): His rule is both real and free of every flaw.

verses.text: So exalted is Allah, the Sovereign, the Truth; there is no deity except Him, Lord of the Noble Throne.

3.reflection: Your home, your phone, your time, even your body: everything you call "mine" has been lent to you for a season. Al-Malik invites you to handle what you hold with the care of someone looking after another's property. When the fear of losing something grips you, remembering that it was never truly yours can lighten the load. Living as a trustee protects you from both arrogance and anxiety.
3.practice: Today, take care of one thing you use or have been entrusted with as if you were looking after it for its real owner.

4.name: Al-Quddus
4.meaning: The Most Pure, utterly free of every flaw and imperfection.
4.description:
Al-Quddus comes from the root q-d-s, which carries the meaning of purity, cleanness and holiness. Jerusalem's Arabic name, al-Quds, the Qur'anic phrase "the holy land" and the title Ruh al-Qudus given to Gabriel all come from this root.

Al-Quddus is the One beyond every deficiency, fault, error and limitation the human mind might imagine. To call on Allah by this name is to declare Him far above any likeness to creation and anything unworthy of Him. It is closely tied to the meaning of the phrase SubhanAllah.

The name appears twice in the Qur'an, in Al-Hashr 59:23 and Al-Jumu'ah 62:1. In both verses it comes directly after Al-Malik, showing that His sovereignty is pure: untouched by injustice, error or lack.

verses.text: Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth is exalting Allah, the Sovereign, the Pure, the Exalted in Might, the Wise.

4.reflection: Purity is not only about what is on the outside; it lives in your thoughts, your words and your intentions. Al-Quddus invites you to let go of the resentments, envy and clutter that weigh you down. Notice one thing crowding your mind today and try setting it aside. Sometimes becoming clean is not about adding something, but about releasing it.
4.practice: Clear out one space today, your desk, your bag or your phone, and remove what you no longer need.

5.name: As-Salam
5.meaning: The Source of Peace, free of all defect and the Giver of safety.
5.description:
As-Salam comes from the root s-l-m, meaning soundness, safety, wholeness, peace and surrender. The words Islam and Muslim share this root. As-Salam is both the One who is free of every flaw and the One from whom peace and well-being flow.

The name has two sides. First, there is no defect, harm or deficiency in His being or His actions. Second, He grants peace and tranquility to His servants. When Muslims greet one another with "as-salamu alaykum," they carry this name and its meaning into everyday life.

The name As-Salam appears in Al-Hashr 59:23. Paradise is called Dar as-Salam, the Home of Peace (Yunus 10:25, Al-An'am 6:127), and Surah Al-Qadr describes the Night of Decree as peace until the break of dawn.

verses.text: He is Allah, other than whom there is no deity, the Sovereign, the Pure, the Perfection, the Grantor of Security, the Overseer, the Exalted in Might, the Compeller, the Superior. Exalted is Allah above whatever they associate with Him.
And Allah invites to the Home of Peace [i.e., Paradise] and guides whom He wills to a straight path.

5.reflection: To greet someone with peace is to tell them, "You have nothing to fear from me." As-Salam reminds you that peace can begin in your own words and manner. In a tense room today, be the first to speak gently. Sometimes one calm sentence is enough to change the air.
5.practice: Be the first to greet someone today with whom things have grown cold.

6.name: Al-Mu'min
6.meaning: The Giver of Security, who grants safety and confirms His promise.
6.description:
Al-Mu'min comes from the root a-m-n, which carries the sense of safety, trust, freedom from fear, and belief. Amana (trust), amin (trustworthy) and iman (faith) all share this root. Used for people, the word means "believer"; used for Allah, it means the One who grants security and the One who confirms.

The name has two main layers. First, He makes His servants safe from fear and gives them security and calm. Second, He confirms His messengers with clear signs and is true to His word. Allah does not break His promise, so whoever relies on Him knows the ground beneath them is firm.

Al-Mu'min appears as a divine name in Al-Hashr 59:23. The related idea of amn, security, runs through many verses; Al-An'am 6:82 teaches that true security belongs to those who do not mix their faith with wrongdoing.

verses.text: He is Allah, other than whom there is no deity, the Sovereign, the Pure, the Perfection, the Grantor of Security, the Overseer, the Exalted in Might, the Compeller, the Superior. Exalted is Allah above whatever they associate with Him.
They who believe and do not mix their belief with injustice - those will have security, and they are [rightly] guided.

6.reflection: Being trustworthy is one of the most precious qualities a person can carry. Al-Mu'min points you to the true source of security, and reminds you that you can be a safe harbor for others too. Even the small promises you keep build someone's trust in you. Today, try closing the gap between what you say and what you do.
6.practice: Keep one small promise or appointment today that you have been putting off, exactly as you said you would.

7.name: Al-Muhaymin
7.meaning: The Guardian, who watches over, protects and bears witness to all things.
7.description:
Al-Muhaymin is derived from the root h-y-m-n, though some linguists link it to a-m-n, the root of security and trust. The word means to watch over, to guard, to oversee and to bear witness.

Al-Muhaymin is the One who knows and keeps watch over the deeds, words, provision and lifespan of every creature. This watchfulness is not a threat but a form of care and protection: nothing lies outside His knowledge and nothing is left to drift.

The name appears for Allah in Al-Hashr 59:23. The same word is used in Al-Ma'idah 5:48 to describe the Qur'an as a guardian over the scriptures before it, confirming them and watching over them. That usage makes the protective and confirming sense of the word especially clear.

verses.text: He is Allah, other than whom there is no deity, the Sovereign, the Pure, the Perfection, the Grantor of Security, the Overseer, the Exalted in Might, the Compeller, the Superior. Exalted is Allah above whatever they associate with Him.

7.reflection: Who you are when you think no one is watching says a lot about who you really are. Al-Muhaymin reminds you that none of your moments go unseen, which is both a responsibility and a comfort. Your efforts are never wasted, even when no one notices them. Today, try doing your work with care even when nobody is looking.
7.practice: Finish one task today that no one will notice, with the same care you would give if everyone were watching.

8.name: Al-Aziz
8.meaning: The Almighty, invincible in power and matchless in honor.
8.description:
Al-Aziz comes from the root a-z-z, which means to be strong, to prevail and to be undefeated, and also to be rare and precious. The word izza, meaning honor, dignity and might, shares this root.

Al-Aziz is the One whom no power can resist, who has no equal and who needs no one. The name speaks both of His unconquerable strength and of His uniqueness and worth. True honor comes from Him, and human dignity is found in nearness to Him and in integrity.

Al-Aziz appears very often in the Qur'an, usually paired with Al-Hakim (the Wise) or Ar-Rahim (the Merciful). The pairing is meaningful: His might is always joined with wisdom and mercy. In Surah Ash-Shu'ara the line "indeed, your Lord is the Exalted in Might, the Merciful" returns again and again, and Al-Munafiqun 63:8 declares that honor belongs to Allah, His Messenger and the believers.

verses.text: And indeed, your Lord - He is the Exalted in Might, the Merciful.

Say, "O Allah, Owner of Sovereignty, You give sovereignty to whom You will and You take sovereignty away from whom You will. You honor whom You will and You humble whom You will. In Your hand is [all] good. Indeed, You are over all things competent. …

8.reflection: Dignity is not won by making others small, but by standing firm where you know you are right. Al-Aziz reminds you that real worth is not found in titles or applause, but in nearness to Him. When someone's words make you feel worthless, remember that their words are not the source of your value. As you guard your own dignity, remember to guard other people's too.
8.practice: When someone who is not present is being talked about today, say one thing that protects their dignity.

9.name: Al-Jabbar
9.meaning: The Restorer, who mends what is broken and whose will prevails.
9.description:
Al-Jabbar comes from the root j-b-r, whose earliest meaning is to set a broken bone and bind it so it heals; a splint is called jabira. The root also carries the senses of setting things right by force, of carrying out one's will, and of loftiness.

The name holds meanings that complete one another: Allah mends broken hearts, makes up what is lacking, sets right what has gone wrong, and nothing can resist His will. His power is not for oppression, but for repair and for putting things in their proper place.

Al-Jabbar appears as a divine name in Al-Hashr 59:23. When the same word describes human beings, however, it turns negative and means a tyrant; the Qur'an notes that neither John nor Jesus was jabbar (Maryam 19:14, 19:32). The contrast shows that such power is flawless only in Allah.

verses.text: He is Allah, other than whom there is no deity, the Sovereign, the Pure, the Perfection, the Grantor of Security, the Overseer, the Exalted in Might, the Compeller, the Superior. Exalted is Allah above whatever they associate with Him.

9.reflection: There may be something in your life that is broken, unfinished or gone wrong. Al-Jabbar reminds you that broken things can be mended and that no loss is the final word. Today you can play a small part in binding up someone else's hurt. Mending often begins with simply listening.
9.practice: Call someone you know is hurting today, ask how they are, and simply listen.

10.name: Al-Mutakabbir
10.meaning: The Supreme in Greatness, to whom all majesty belongs.
10.description:
Al-Mutakabbir comes from the root k-b-r, meaning to be great and exalted. The word akbar in "Allahu akbar" and kibriya (majesty) come from the same root. Al-Mutakabbir is the One to whom greatness and grandeur truly belong.

The name teaches that greatness befits Allah alone. When the same root describes human beings, as kibr (arrogance), it is a blameworthy trait, because a person who acts grand is claiming a quality that is not theirs. Allah's greatness, by contrast, is real: everything is His creation, and nothing is equal to Him.

Al-Mutakabbir appears as a divine name in Al-Hashr 59:23. Al-Jathiyah 45:37 declares that all grandeur in the heavens and the earth belongs to Him, while many other verses criticize those who think themselves great and turn away from the truth.

verses.text: He is Allah, other than whom there is no deity, the Sovereign, the Pure, the Perfection, the Grantor of Security, the Overseer, the Exalted in Might, the Compeller, the Superior. Exalted is Allah above whatever they associate with Him.
And to Him belongs [all] grandeur within the heavens and the earth, and He is the Exalted in Might, the Wise.

10.reflection: Knowing that true greatness belongs only to Him is both freeing and simplifying. You do not have to know everything, win every argument or always be right. Al-Mutakabbir releases you from the exhausting work of seeming bigger than you are. Today, try the lightness that comes with saying, "I was wrong."
10.practice: On some small matter where you were mistaken today, tell the other person, "You're right, I was wrong."

11.name: Al-Khaliq
11.meaning: The Creator, who determines all things by measure and brings them into being.
11.description:
Al-Khaliq comes from the root kh-l-q, whose earliest meaning is to measure and determine; from there it came to mean bringing something into existence. The words khalq (creation, created beings) and akhlaq (character, one's innate dispositions) share this root.

Al-Khaliq is the One who sets out everything according to a plan and a measure, and then brings it into being. Creation begins with determination: what each thing will be, how it will be, and in what proportion. This name reminds us that the universe reflects order and meaning rather than randomness.

The name appears in many verses as "the Creator of all things" (Al-An'am 6:102, Ar-Ra'd 13:16, Az-Zumar 39:62). In Al-Hashr 59:24 it is listed with Al-Bari' and Al-Musawwir, almost as if describing the stages of creation. The intensive form Al-Khallaq, from the same root, appears in Al-Hijr 15:86 and Ya-Sin 36:81.

verses.text: That is Allah, your Lord; there is no deity except Him, the Creator of all things, so worship Him. And He is Disposer of all things.

11.reflection: Remembering that everything around you was created with measure can change how you see it. The veins of a leaf, a baby's fingers, the order of the sky: each carries the trace of a design. Al-Khaliq reminds you that you are part of this order too, and that you were not created without purpose. Today, try pausing to truly look at one detail of creation.
11.practice: Spend one full minute today carefully watching a plant, an insect or the sky.

12.name: Al-Bari'
12.meaning: The Maker, who brings creation into being flawless, distinct and in harmony.
12.description:
Al-Bari' comes from the root b-r-', which means to create and bring into being, and also to be free of or clear from something. The words bariyya (creation, all created beings) and bari' (free, innocent) share this root.

Al-Bari' is the One who brings creatures into existence distinct from one another, free of defect and in harmony with each other. Where Al-Khaliq emphasizes determining and measuring, Al-Bari' emphasizes bringing that decree into existence complete and balanced. The unique makeup of every being reflects this name.

In the Qur'an, Al-Bari' appears in Al-Hashr 59:24 between Al-Khaliq and Al-Musawwir. In Al-Baqarah 2:54, Moses tells his people to repent to their Maker (Bari'). Surah Al-Bayyinah calls those who believe and do good khayr al-bariyya, the best of creation.

verses.text: He is Allah, the Creator, the Producer, the Fashioner; to Him belong the best names. Whatever is in the heavens and earth is exalting Him. And He is the Exalted in Might, the Wise.

12.reflection: There is no one else in the world exactly like you: your voice, your gaze and your inner world are your own. Al-Bari' reminds you that this difference is not a defect but a sign of care. When comparing yourself to others leaves you feeling less, remember that being made differently has meaning too. Try looking at other people's differences with the same respect.
12.practice: Tell someone whose views or style differ from yours about one thing you genuinely admire in them.

13.name: Al-Musawwir
13.meaning: The Fashioner, who gives every being its unique form and shape.
13.description:
Al-Musawwir comes from the root s-w-r, meaning form, shape and appearance. The words sura (form, image) and tasawwur (picturing something in the mind) share this root. Al-Musawwir is the One who shapes and fashions.

Al-Khaliq, Al-Bari' and Al-Musawwir are often explained together as stages of creation: determining, bringing into being and giving form. Al-Musawwir describes the final step, granting each being the particular appearance and structure that sets it apart. That no two faces, fingerprints or leaves are exactly alike opens a door to reflecting on this name.

The name appears in Al-Hashr 59:24. Verbs from the same root appear in many verses about human creation: Aal-Imran 3:6 speaks of being shaped in the womb, while At-Taghabun 64:3 and Ghafir 40:64 remind us of the beautiful form given to human beings.

verses.text: He is Allah, the Creator, the Producer, the Fashioner; to Him belong the best names. Whatever is in the heavens and earth is exalting Him. And He is the Exalted in Might, the Wise.
It is He who forms you in the wombs however He wills. There is no deity except Him, the Exalted in Might, the Wise.

13.reflection: The face you see in the mirror is a form given with care. Al-Musawwir invites you to look at your body and appearance with gratitude rather than criticism. When you get stuck on something you dislike about yourself, remember that it too is part of that care. Today, try looking at yourself and others with a gentler eye.
13.practice: When you look in the mirror today, instead of searching for flaws, give thanks for one thing your body allows you to do.

14.name: Al-Ghaffar
14.meaning: The Ever-Forgiving, who covers and pardons faults again and again.
14.description:
Al-Ghaffar comes from the root gh-f-r, whose first meaning is to cover or conceal; a helmet that protects the head in battle is called a mighfar. Maghfira is the covering and pardoning of wrongdoing.

The intensive fa''al pattern of Al-Ghaffar stresses how often and how repeatedly forgiveness is given: each time a person returns and regrets, they are forgiven anew. The name also speaks of dignity being preserved as faults are covered. Allah does not only pardon His servant's mistake; He covers it without exposing it.

Al-Ghaffar appears in verses such as Ta-Ha 20:82, Sad 38:66, Az-Zumar 39:5, Ghafir 40:42 and Nuh 71:10, while the related name Al-Ghafur appears very frequently. Noah's call to his people in Nuh 71:10 to seek forgiveness shows the hopeful face of this name.

verses.text: And said, 'Ask forgiveness of your Lord. Indeed, He is ever a Perpetual Forgiver. …
But indeed, I am the Perpetual Forgiver of whoever repents and believes and does righteousness and then continues in guidance.

14.reflection: A past mistake may still be circling in your mind. Al-Ghaffar reminds you that the door of return never closes and that a fresh start is always possible. As someone who hopes to be forgiven, you can choose to cover other people's faults rather than expose them. Today, try covering a mistake instead of magnifying it.
14.practice: When you notice someone's small mistake today, let it pass without pointing it out in front of others.

15.name: Al-Qahhar
15.meaning: The Subduer, who prevails over all and whom no power can resist.
15.description:
Al-Qahhar comes from the root q-h-r, meaning to prevail, to overcome and to bring into submission. Its intensive fa''al pattern stresses that this supremacy is complete and unbroken.

Al-Qahhar is the One whom no power can withstand and to whose will everything yields. The name reminds us that the fears, tyrannies and self-important powers that press down on people are, in truth, limited. It also suggests that a person can ask Him for strength against their own harmful impulses.

Wherever Al-Qahhar appears in the Qur'an, it is paired with Al-Wahid, the One: Yusuf 12:39, Ar-Ra'd 13:16, Ibrahim 14:48, Sad 38:65, Az-Zumar 39:4 and Ghafir 40:16. The pairing teaches that true and absolute supremacy can belong only to the One who has no partner.

verses.text: O [my] two companions of prison, are separate lords better or Allah, the One, the Prevailing?
The Day they come forth nothing concerning them will be concealed from Allah. To whom belongs [all] sovereignty this Day? To Allah, the One, the Prevailing.

15.reflection: There may be a situation or a person that frightens you or looms large. Al-Qahhar reminds you that no power is absolute and that His authority stands over all. Holding onto this gives you the courage to do what is right without letting fear freeze you. Today, take one small step against a habit that has a hold on you.
15.practice: Today, deliberately put off a draining habit (like mindless scrolling) once, and win that round.

16.name: Al-Wahhab
16.meaning: The Bestower, who gives freely and abundantly without expecting anything in return.
16.description:
Al-Wahhab comes from the root w-h-b, which means to give freely, to give as a gift. The words hiba (gift) and mawhiba (endowment, talent) share this root. The intensive fa''al pattern stresses that this giving is abundant, continuous and unconditional.

People usually give to one another hoping for something back, whether thanks, return or benefit. Al-Wahhab gives without expecting anything and often before being asked. Life, our abilities, the people we love and our capacity to understand are all examples of His gifts.

The name appears in Aal-Imran 3:8, Sad 38:9 and Sad 38:35. Many prophetic prayers in the Qur'an begin with "grant me" (hab li): Zechariah asking for a child (Aal-Imran 3:38), Solomon for a kingdom (Sad 38:35) and Abraham for wisdom (Ash-Shu'ara 26:83).

verses.text: [Who say], "Our Lord, let not our hearts deviate after You have guided us and grant us from Yourself mercy. Indeed, You are the Bestower. …

16.reflection: Most of your talents, the people you love and the good moments you have lived came to you without your asking. Al-Wahhab invites you to notice that your life is a chain of gifts. That awareness also loosens the habit of keeping accounts when you give. Today, try the lightness of giving without expecting anything back.
16.practice: Take on a task for someone today without expecting anything in return, not even thanks.

17.name: Ar-Razzaq
17.meaning: The Provider, who creates and grants sustenance to every living being.
17.description:
Ar-Razzaq comes from the root r-z-q. Rizq refers to everything a living being benefits from: not only food and drink, but also knowledge, a sound mind, peace of heart and good relationships. The intensive fa''al pattern stresses how continuous and generous this provision is.

The name reminds us that the true source of provision is Allah. People work, make an effort and take the means available to them, but it is He who brings about the result and gives blessing to it. This awareness protects a person from both idleness and the restless greed that worry about provision can breed.

Ar-Razzaq appears in Adh-Dhariyat 51:58. Hud 11:6 declares that the provision of every creature on earth rests with Allah, and several verses call Him khayr ar-raziqin, the best of providers.

verses.text: Indeed, it is Allah who is the [continual] Provider, the firm possessor of strength.

17.reflection: Worry about provision is often among a person's deepest anxieties. Ar-Razzaq reminds you to give your effort fully while not carrying the weight of the outcome alone. Consider that what reaches you may also be a means for it to reach others. Today, try noticing the long journey behind the food on your table.
17.practice: Share part of one of your meals today with a neighbor or a colleague.

18.name: Al-Fattah
18.meaning: The Opener, who opens closed doors, eases hardship and judges with truth.
18.description:
Al-Fattah comes from the root f-t-h, meaning to open: to open a door, to open a city, to resolve a problem, and to settle a matter between two parties by judging between them. The words fath (opening, victory), miftah (key) and Fatiha (the Opening) all share this root.

Al-Fattah is the One who opens the doors of mercy and provision, untangles difficulties, clears paths that seemed closed and judges between people with truth. The intensive fa''al pattern stresses that these openings are many and ongoing. The name reminds us that a way out can be found from both material and inner hardship.

Al-Fattah appears in Saba 34:26 together with Al-Alim. In Al-A'raf 7:89 He is addressed as "the best of those who give decision." Fatir 35:2 declares that no one can hold back the mercy He opens, and Al-An'am 6:59 states that the keys of the unseen are with Him alone.

verses.text: Say, "Our Lord will bring us together; then He will judge between us in truth. And He is the Knowing Judge."
Whatever Allah grants to people of mercy - none can withhold it; and whatever He withholds - none can release it thereafter. And He is the Exalted in Might, the Wise.

18.reflection: At times it may feel as if every door in front of you is shut. Al-Fattah reminds you that an opening can come from a place you never expected. Your part is to try the key in your hand and not lose hope. Today you can help open a small door for someone else, too.
18.practice: Help clear an obstacle for someone today by sharing a job lead, a piece of know-how or a useful contact.

19.name: Al-Alim
19.meaning: The All-Knowing, who fully knows the hidden and the manifest.
19.description:
Al-Alim comes from the root a-l-m, meaning to know and to grasp the reality of something. The words ilm (knowledge), alim (scholar) and alam (sign, marker) share this root. The fa'il pattern stresses that this knowledge is comprehensive, deep and permanent.

Al-Alim is the One who knows past, present and future, the seen and the unseen, what is spoken aloud and what is hidden in hearts, completely and without gaps. Human knowledge is acquired, limited and open to error; Allah's knowledge has no limits. The name brings both humility and reassurance: there are things you do not know, but nothing lies outside His knowledge.

Al-Alim is among the most frequently occurring names in the Qur'an and is usually paired with Al-Hakim (the Wise), As-Sami' (the All-Hearing) or Al-Khabir (the All-Aware). In Al-Baqarah 2:32, the angels confess, "we have no knowledge except what You have taught us," a beautiful reminder of where knowledge truly comes from.

verses.text: They said, "Exalted are You; we have no knowledge except what You have taught us. Indeed, it is You who is the Knowing, the Wise."

19.reflection: You do not have to know everything; saying "I don't know" is a virtue too. Al-Alim reminds you that knowledge is a trust and that everything you learn opens a new door. Your inner world, which you may feel no one understands, is fully known to Him, so you need not feel alone in it. Today, set aside a little time to learn something you are curious about.
19.practice: Ask someone a question today about something you don't know, without feeling embarrassed.

20.name: Al-Qabid
20.meaning: The Withholder, who constricts and holds back according to His wisdom.
20.description:
Al-Qabid comes from the root q-b-d, meaning to grasp in the hand, to hold, to constrict and to draw back. Al-Qabid is the One who, by His wisdom, holds back, narrows and limits what He wills.

This name is usually reflected on together with the name that follows it, Al-Basit (the Expander). Provision, opportunities and the course of life sometimes narrow and sometimes widen, and both lie within His decree and wisdom. Constriction is not a punishment or a sign of being forgotten; often it is a season that invites a person to pause, reflect, be patient and turn back to Him.

The name Al-Qabid does not occur in this exact form in the Qur'an; it entered the list of the Beautiful Names through hadith narrations. Its meaning, however, is stated plainly in Al-Baqarah 2:245: "it is Allah who withholds and grants abundance." Verses such as Ar-Ra'd 13:26 and Al-Isra 17:30 likewise teach that the widening and narrowing of provision is in His hands.

verses.text: Who is it that would loan Allah a goodly loan so He may multiply it for him many times over? And it is Allah who withholds and grants abundance, and to Him you will be returned.

20.reflection: Some seasons of your life may feel narrow and difficult; that does not mean the road has ended. Al-Qabid reminds you that constriction, like expansion, carries wisdom and does not last forever. In tight times you come to value what you have and let go of what you do not need more easily. Today, try looking at a difficulty you are facing and asking what it is inviting you toward.
20.practice: Write down one situation that is weighing on you today, and beneath it note one thing it has taught you.

21.name: Al-Basit
21.meaning: The One who expands and extends provision, mercy and relief as He wills.
21.description:
Al-Basit comes from the Arabic root b-s-t, meaning to open, spread out or extend. The same root describes opening one's hand, unrolling a carpet, or a heart that feels at ease. The name speaks of Allah widening provision, mercy, opportunity and inner peace for whomever He wills, in the measure He wills.

It is traditionally paired with Al-Qabid, the One who withholds. The Qur'an does not use Al-Basit as a noun title, but the verb appears often: "It is Allah who withholds and grants abundance." Expansion and constriction may look like opposites, yet both flow from the same wisdom. Surah Ash-Shura reminds us that provision is sent down in measure, and that unlimited abundance does not always lead to good.

This name points to where every blessing comes from, and to the meaning of passing it on. Whoever opens to others what has been opened to them lives out something of this name.

verses.text: Who is it that would loan Allah a goodly loan so He may multiply it for him many times over? And it is Allah who withholds and grants abundance, and to Him you will be returned.

And if Allah had extended [excessively] provision for His servants, they would have committed tyranny throughout the earth. But He sends [it] down in an amount which He wills. Indeed He is, of His servants, Aware and Seeing.

21.reflection: Look at the areas of your life where you feel room to breathe: your time, your health, a friendship, an opportunity. None of these are purely your own doing; they are doors that were opened for you. In a season of tightness, you can remember that a closed door may simply be one whose time has not yet come. And when openness is a trust, opening it to others becomes part of your share.
21.practice: Today, generously share something you have, whether a skill, a resource or some of your time, with someone who needs it.

22.name: Al-Khafid
22.meaning: The One who, in His wisdom, lowers whom He wills and brings down arrogance.
22.description:
Al-Khafid comes from the root kh-f-d, meaning to lower, bring down or soften. The same root appears in the Qur'an in the command to "lower the wing of humility" toward one's parents out of mercy (Al-Isra 17:24). So the root carries not only the idea of descent, but also gentleness and humility.

In the traditional lists of the Beautiful Names, Al-Khafid is paired with Ar-Rafi'. It does not appear in the Qur'an as a title, but Surah Al-Waqi'ah describes the Day of Judgment as one that will bring some down and raise others up. People will find their place not by their worldly rank, but by their true worth. In the verse, it is the Event itself that brings down and raises up; its link to the name Al-Khafid lies in this overwhelming event coming about by Allah's decree.

This name is not meant to frighten, but to restore a sense of balance: no position lasts forever, and no arrogance brings real height. Allah's lowering is always just and wise; no one is wronged.

verses.text: It will bring down [some] and raise up [others].

22.reflection: Sometimes a disappointment, a loss or an unexpected setback sets you down on firmer ground. The moments when you start to feel above others are often the moments you are most fragile. Try seeing humility today not as a loss, but as a gain. A head bowed by choice stands taller than anyone could force it to.
22.practice: Today, in one conversation, choose to truly listen instead of proving that you are right.

23.name: Ar-Rafi'
23.meaning: The One who raises whom He wills, degree by degree.
23.description:
Ar-Rafi' comes from the root r-f-', meaning to lift, raise or elevate. It is used for lifting something off the ground, raising the foundations of a building, or elevating someone's standing.

The Qur'an speaks often of Allah raising people up. Surah Al-Mujadilah promises that Allah will raise, by degrees, those who believe and those who have been given knowledge, and it's striking that this promise comes alongside something as ordinary as making room for others in a gathering. Surah Ghafir describes Allah as the One "exalted above all degrees" (Ghafir 40:15).

Ar-Rafi' is understood together with Al-Khafid. True elevation does not come from status or fame, but from faith, knowledge, character and the kindness we show others.

verses.text: O you who have believed, when you are told, "Space yourselves" in assemblies, then make space; Allah will make space for you. And when you are told, "Arise," then arise; Allah will raise those who have believed among you and those who were given knowledge, by degrees. And Allah is Aware of what you do.

23.reflection: When you think of rising, you might picture titles, achievements or visibility. Yet the Qur'an ties rising in rank to knowledge and to a small courtesy like making room for someone else. The time you spend learning today, and the space you open for another person, lift you in the truest sense. You never need to lower anyone in order to rise.
23.practice: Today, make space for someone whose voice is rarely heard, whether in a meeting, a conversation or a group.

24.name: Al-Mu'izz
24.meaning: The One who grants honor, dignity and strength to whom He wills.
24.description:
Al-Mu'izz comes from the root '-z-z, meaning to be strong, invincible and precious. From it comes 'izzah: honor, dignity and might. The name Al-Aziz shares this root. Al-Mu'izz is the One who bestows that honor on others.

The name does not appear in the Qur'an as a title, but its meaning is clear in the supplication of Surah Aal-Imran: "You honor whom You will." Surah Fatir adds that all honor belongs to Allah, and that good words and righteous deeds rise up to Him.

This name invites you to ask where you look for your dignity. Real honor is not fed by the approval or power of others, but by truthfulness and goodness.

verses.text: Say, "O Allah, Owner of Sovereignty, You give sovereignty to whom You will and You take sovereignty away from whom You will. You honor whom You will and You humble whom You will. In Your hand is [all] good. Indeed, You are over all things competent. …

Whoever desires honor [through power] - then to Allah belongs all honor. To Him ascends good speech, and righteous work raises it. But they who plot evil deeds will have a severe punishment, and the plotting of those - it will perish.

24.reflection: Think about whose approval you need in order to feel worthy. Dignity that depends on how others see you can crumble at the slightest criticism. The respect that comes from honest words and good conduct is an honor no one can take away. When you honor someone else today, you are protecting your own dignity as well.
24.practice: Today, sincerely acknowledge someone's effort or a good quality of theirs, in front of them.

25.name: Al-Mudhill
25.meaning: The One who, in His justice and wisdom, takes honor away from whom He wills.
25.description:
Al-Mudhill comes from the root dh-l-l, meaning to become lowly or to lose one's strength and standing. The same root appears in a positive sense in the Qur'an, in "the wing of humility" one lowers toward one's parents (Al-Isra 17:24). The root holds both the idea of being brought low and that of gentle humility.

Al-Mudhill is paired with Al-Mu'izz and does not appear in the Qur'an as a title. Its meaning is found in the supplication of Surah Aal-Imran: "You honor whom You will and You humble whom You will. In Your hand is [all] good." It is worth noticing that the verse continues with "in Your hand is [all] good": both honor and humbling are decreed with wisdom.

The Qur'an reminds us that Allah does not wrong people in the slightest; it is people who often wrong themselves through their own choices. This name teaches that arrogance and injustice bring no lasting advantage, and that everything is subject to divine justice.

verses.text: Say, "O Allah, Owner of Sovereignty, You give sovereignty to whom You will and You take sovereignty away from whom You will. You honor whom You will and You humble whom You will. In Your hand is [all] good. Indeed, You are over all things competent. …
Indeed, Allah does not wrong the people at all, but it is the people who are wronging themselves.

25.reflection: When reflecting on this name, it is more meaningful to turn your gaze inward rather than toward others. Arrogance, injustice or stubbornness quietly wear away a person's own worth. Noticing the habits that diminish you is the first step to letting them go. Bowing in humility never makes you smaller; it helps you grow.
25.practice: Today, openly own up to a mistake or a moment when you were unfair, and apologize if it's needed.

26.name: As-Sami'
26.meaning: The One who fully hears every sound, every word and every prayer.
26.description:
As-Sami' comes from the root s-m-', meaning to hear, and its intensive form conveys "the One who hears completely and perfectly." His hearing depends on no organ and no distance; what is spoken aloud and what is only whispered in the heart are equally known to Him.

The name appears more than forty times in the Qur'an, usually paired with Al-Alim or Al-Basir. In Surah Al-Baqarah, Abraham and Ishmael pray as they raise the foundations of the Ka'bah: "Indeed, You are the Hearing, the Knowing." Surah Al-Mujadilah opens by telling us that Allah heard the words of a woman who brought her complaint to Him.

This name is both a comfort and a responsibility: no prayer goes unheard, and no word is spoken in vain.

verses.text: And [mention] when Abraham was raising the foundations of the House and [with him] Ishmael, [saying], "Our Lord, accept [this] from us. Indeed, You are the Hearing, the Knowing. …

And when My servants ask you, [O Muhammad], concerning Me - indeed I am near. I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me. So let them respond to Me [by obedience] and believe in Me that they may be [rightly] guided.

26.reflection: Even when it feels like no one understands you, knowing that you are heard can make the loneliness lighter. A wish you only thought, a worry you never told anyone, is heard as well. In the same way, remembering that every word you say is heard can help you choose your words with care. Today, try truly listening to someone; they may need to be heard too.
26.practice: Today, put your phone aside while someone is talking to you and listen without interrupting until they finish.

27.name: Al-Basir
27.meaning: The One who fully sees all things, hidden and apparent.
27.description:
Al-Basir comes from the root b-s-r, meaning to see and to perceive. The word basirah, meaning deep insight, shares the same root. The name expresses that nothing lies outside His sight.

Al-Basir appears in many verses of the Qur'an, often alongside As-Sami'. In Surah Ash-Shura, right after "There is nothing like unto Him" comes "and He is the Hearing, the Seeing", a reminder that His seeing is unlike that of any creature. Surah Al-Mulk points to birds spreading and folding their wings in the sky to show how His sight encompasses every detail.

This name both reassures you that you are never alone and invites sincerity in what you do. A kindness no one else notices has still been seen.

verses.text: Do they not see the birds above them with wings outspread and [sometimes] folded in? None holds them [aloft] except the Most Merciful. Indeed He is, of all things, Seeing.

[He is] Creator of the heavens and the earth. He has made for you from yourselves, mates, and among the cattle, mates; He multiplies you thereby. There is nothing like unto Him, and He is the Hearing, the Seeing.

27.reflection: Don't assume that a good deed nobody noticed was wasted; it was seen. Don't assume that a hardship you carry alone goes unseen either. This awareness helps you live with sincerity rather than for show. Today, try looking a little more closely at the small details around you, like a bird in flight or the tired face of someone near you.
27.practice: Today, do a small kindness that no one will see or know about.

28.name: Al-Hakam
28.meaning: The Judge who rules with truth and gives the final, just verdict.
28.description:
Al-Hakam comes from the root h-k-m, meaning to judge, to distinguish, and to restrain. At its core, the root means preventing corruption and injustice. The words hukm (ruling), hikmah (wisdom) and hakim (judge) all share it. Al-Hakam is the One who separates right from wrong and restores what is due.

The name appears clearly in Surah Al-An'am: "Is it other than Allah I should seek as judge?" The Qur'an also advises appointing arbitrators in disputes (An-Nisa 4:35), showing that fair arbitration between people is itself a valued task.

Al-Hakam reminds us not to rush our own judgments. The final and certain judgment belongs to Him; our part is to strive to be fair and balanced.

verses.text: [Say], "Then is it other than Allah I should seek as judge while it is He who has revealed to you the Book [i.e., the Qur'an] explained in detail?" And those to whom We [previously] gave the Scripture know that it is sent down from your Lord in truth, so never be among the doubters.

28.reflection: You make countless judgments every day, often without noticing: about people, about events, even about yourself. How many of them are hasty, or built on incomplete information? Knowing that the final judgment belongs to Him frees you from the burden of judging everyone and helps you become more understanding. Hearing both sides before taking one in a disagreement is a small reflection of this name in your life.
28.practice: Today, when you're about to make a quick judgment about someone, pause and try to understand their point of view.

29.name: Al-Adl
29.meaning: The Perfectly Just, who never wrongs anyone in any way.
29.description:
Al-Adl comes from the root '-d-l, meaning to be equal, to balance, to be upright and fair. It describes the two pans of a scale sitting level. The name takes the form of a verbal noun, which emphasizes that Allah's justice is not merely an attribute He has, but that He is justice itself.

Al-Adl does not appear in the Qur'an as a title, yet justice is among the Qur'an's most central themes. Surah An-Nahl declares that Allah commands justice and good conduct. Surah Al-An'am states that the word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and in justice.

This name reminds us that every balance and every right in the world rests on His justice. To the extent that a person keeps the measure and gives each their due, they carry a reflection of this justice into their life.

verses.text: Indeed, Allah orders justice and good conduct and giving [help] to relatives and forbids immorality and bad conduct and oppression. He admonishes you that perhaps you will be reminded.
And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and in justice. None can alter His words, and He is the Hearing, the Knowing.

29.reflection: Justice doesn't live only in courtrooms; it lives in the small moments of daily life: dividing up a task, handling a disagreement, treating children or colleagues. It is easy to favor someone you love or to be unfair to someone you don't. Today, try to keep an eye on both sides of the scale. Giving someone their due, even when it costs you, is the hardest and most valuable form of justice.
29.practice: Today, say what is right or give someone their due, even if it doesn't work in your favor.

30.name: Al-Latif
30.meaning: The Subtle One who knows the finest details and is gentle and kind to His servants.
30.description:
Al-Latif comes from the root l-t-f, meaning to be fine, gentle, hidden and graceful. The name holds two layers of meaning: knowing the most hidden and delicate of things, and doing good to His servants in ways so subtle they often go unnoticed.

Al-Latif usually appears in the Qur'an alongside Al-Khabir. Surah Al-An'am says that vision cannot perceive Him, while He perceives all vision. Surah Ash-Shura highlights that Allah is subtle and kind with His servants. When Joseph, after years of separation and hardship, says "Indeed, my Lord is Subtle in what He wills" (Yusuf 12:100), we see the trace of this name within a human life.

This name reminds us that behind the visible surface of events, a quiet kindness may be at work.

verses.text: Allah is Subtle with His servants; He gives provision to whom He wills. And He is the Powerful, the Exalted in Might.
Vision perceives Him not, but He perceives [all] vision; and He is the Subtle, the Aware.

30.reflection: Have you ever looked back and realized that something painful at the time later carried you somewhere good? Kindness often arrives quietly: a coincidence, a new acquaintance, a word spoken at just the right time. Today, try to notice these silent gifts in your life. You too can help someone gently, without making them feel embarrassed.
30.practice: Today, show someone a small kindness without drawing attention to yourself or embarrassing them.

31.name: Al-Khabir
31.meaning: The All-Aware, who knows the inner reality and hidden sides of all things.
31.description:
Al-Khabir comes from the root kh-b-r, meaning to be informed and to know the inner nature of something. The everyday Arabic word for news, khabar, shares this root. But the knowledge meant here is not news received from outside; it is a deep knowing that reaches the essence of a thing, its true intention and its outcome.

Al-Khabir appears frequently in the Qur'an, often alongside Al-Latif, Al-Hakim or Al-Alim. Surah Al-Mulk asks, "Does He who created not know?", stressing that the Creator knows His creation best. Many verses close with the words "Allah is aware of what you do."

This name invites reflection on the gap between appearance and reality. Others see only the outside; He knows the intentions as well.

verses.text: Does He who created not know, while He is the Subtle, the Aware?

31.reflection: People usually know you by your actions; few know your intentions, your efforts or your inner world. When you are misunderstood, remembering that your intentions are known can bring you peace. At the same time, this name calls you to examine your own intentions honestly. Today, try asking yourself what the real reason is behind something you're doing.
31.practice: Today, before starting an important task, pause for a moment and state your intention to yourself clearly.

32.name: Al-Halim
32.meaning: The Forbearing, who does not hasten to punish and gives time to return.
32.description:
Al-Halim comes from the root h-l-m, meaning to be gentle, to not be carried away by anger, and to meet things with patience. The root also carries the sense of maturity and sound judgment; hilm is the bearing of a mature person who has power, yet does not act in haste.

In the Qur'an, Al-Halim is usually paired with Al-Ghafur, Al-Ghani or Al-Alim. Surah Al-Baqarah teaches that a kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by hurt, and the verse ends by reminding us that Allah is Forbearing. The same quality is attributed to Prophet Abraham (At-Tawbah 9:114).

This name teaches trust in His patience and gentleness toward others.

verses.text: Kind speech and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury. And Allah is Free of need and Forbearing.

32.reflection: It is easy to react right away when someone makes a mistake; waiting and trying to understand takes strength. When you think of the time you have been given despite your own mistakes, offering the same space to others becomes easier. Even delaying your reply by a few minutes when you're angry can change a lot. Gentleness is not weakness; it's a sign of self-mastery.
32.practice: Today, when something makes you angry, take a deep breath and wait a few minutes before you respond.

33.name: Al-Azim
33.meaning: The Magnificent, whose greatness is beyond what minds can grasp.
33.description:
Al-Azim comes from the root '-z-m, meaning to be great, significant and majestic. Al-Azim is the One who is great beyond every limit and measure, in His essence and in His attributes.

In the Qur'an, this name often appears together with Al-Aliyy. Surah Ash-Shura states that whatever is in the heavens and the earth belongs to Him, and that "He is the Most High, the Most Great." Surah Al-Waqi'ah closes with the call: "So exalt the name of your Lord, the Most Great." Ayat al-Kursi ends with the same words (Al-Baqarah 2:255).

This name helps a person see both their own limits and the greatness that surrounds them. Before His greatness, worldly worries return to their true size.

verses.text: To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth, and He is the Most High, the Most Great.
So exalt the name of your Lord, the Most Great.

33.reflection: Try looking at something that worries you from a little distance today. When you look at the sky, the stars or a wide landscape, how big do your troubles seem? Feeling small before such greatness can actually be a relief; you remember that you don't have to carry everything. This awareness brings both humility and peace.
33.practice: Today, step outside for a few minutes, look up at the sky and quietly reflect on the greatness around you.

34.name: Al-Ghafur
34.meaning: The All-Forgiving, who covers faults and forgives again and again.
34.description:
Al-Ghafur comes from the root gh-f-r, meaning to cover, conceal and protect. The Arabic word for a helmet, mighfar, comes from the same root. Maghfirah, forgiveness, means both that a fault is covered and that a person is protected from its harmful consequences. The form ghafur conveys forgiveness that is abundant and deep.

Al-Ghafur is among the names mentioned most often in the Qur'an, usually alongside Ar-Rahim. The verse in Surah Az-Zumar calls out even to those who have transgressed against themselves: "Do not despair of the mercy of Allah." It is known as one of the most hope-giving calls in the Qur'an.

This name reminds us that no mistake condemns a person to hopelessness. It also encourages us to cover the faults of others and to forgive.

verses.text: Say, "O My servants who have transgressed against themselves [by sinning], do not despair of the mercy of Allah. Indeed, Allah forgives all sins. Indeed, it is He who is the Forgiving, the Merciful."

34.reflection: You may still be carrying a mistake from your past. Regret has value, but when it turns into despair, it keeps you stuck. Just as you can hope to be forgiven, you can cover someone else's fault and avoid embarrassing them in front of others. Today, give both yourself and someone else the chance to turn a new page.
34.practice: Today, forgive someone who hurt you in your heart, or choose not to speak about someone's fault to others.

35.name: Ash-Shakur
35.meaning: The Appreciative, who rewards even a small good deed many times over.
35.description:
Ash-Shakur comes from the root sh-k-r, meaning to recognize a kindness, reward it and make it visible. Arabs would call an animal that thrived on very little feed "shakur." The name expresses that Allah never leaves even a small good deed of His servant unrewarded, but returns it many times over.

In the Qur'an, Ash-Shakur usually appears with Al-Ghafur or Al-Halim. Surah At-Taghabun says that a goodly loan given to Allah will be multiplied, and the verse ends: "Allah is most Appreciative and Forbearing." Surah Fatir describes the people of Paradise praising their Lord, who has removed all sorrow from them, with this very name.

This name reminds us that our own gratitude, and our appreciation of others' efforts, carries real value.

verses.text: If you loan Allah a goodly loan, He will multiply it for you and forgive you. And Allah is [most] Appreciative and Forbearing, …
And they will say, "Praise to Allah, who has removed from us [all] sorrow. Indeed, our Lord is Forgiving and Appreciative - …

35.reflection: There may be times when you feel your small acts of kindness don't really matter. Yet no sincere intention and no effort is ever lost. This awareness also asks something of you: to notice the efforts of the people around you and to thank them. Often, a simple thank-you is enough to change someone's day.
35.practice: Today, sincerely thank someone for something they did, at a moment they don't expect it.

36.name: Al-Aliyy
36.meaning: The Most High, exalted in His essence, attributes and power.
36.description:
Al-Aliyy comes from the root '-l-w, meaning to be high and exalted. This highness is not about physical location, but about worth, power and rank. His exaltedness cannot be compared to anything.

Al-Aliyy usually appears in the Qur'an together with Al-Azim or Al-Kabir; Ayat al-Kursi ends with "He is the Most High, the Most Great" (Al-Baqarah 2:255). In Surah Al-Hajj, after stating that Allah is the Truth and that whatever is called upon besides Him is falsehood, the verse affirms that He is the Most High, the Grand.

This name invites a person to lift their gaze toward higher values. Petty calculations and grudges lose their weight beside this exaltedness.

verses.text: That is because Allah is the True Reality, and that which they call upon other than Him is falsehood, and because Allah is the Most High, the Grand.

36.reflection: In the rush of daily life, small arguments and passing anger can take over your whole mind. Reflecting on this name helps you lift your gaze a little higher. When you remember the values you truly hold, some issues simply shrink on their own. Today, you might consider letting go of a grievance for the sake of something higher.
36.practice: Today, instead of continuing a small argument, choose to close it with kindness.

37.name: Al-Kabir
37.meaning: The Great, greater than all things in His being and attributes.
37.description:
Al-Kabir comes from the root k-b-r, meaning to be great. The phrase "Allahu akbar" (Allah is the Greatest) and the word takbir share this root. The name expresses that true greatness belongs to Him alone.

In the Qur'an, Al-Kabir usually appears with Al-Aliyy or Al-Muta'al. Surah Ar-Ra'd describes Him as the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, the Grand, the Exalted. From the same root comes kibr, arrogance, which the Qur'an treats as a flaw in people, because it means claiming a greatness that isn't one's own.

This name reminds a person both of His greatness and of their own measure. If greatness is His, humility is ours.

verses.text: [He is] Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, the Grand, the Exalted.

37.reflection: You may hear the words "Allahu akbar" many times a day. When you reflect on their meaning, you realize that whatever frightens or overwhelms you is not greater than Him. It is also a quiet warning against seeing yourself as bigger than others. Today, try to see something you achieved not as entirely your own, but as an opportunity you were given.
37.practice: Today, when you talk about something you accomplished, mention by name the people who helped you.

38.name: Al-Hafiz
38.meaning: The Preserver, who protects, watches over and keeps all things.
38.description:
Al-Hafiz comes from the root h-f-z, meaning to protect, guard, preserve and memorize. The word hafiz, used for someone who has memorized the Qur'an, comes from the same root. The name expresses that Allah protects all beings, sustains the order of creation and loses nothing.

Al-Hafiz appears directly in several places in the Qur'an; in Surah Hud we read, "Indeed my Lord is, over all things, Guardian." In Surah Yusuf, Jacob, worried about his son, says, "Allah is the best guardian." Surah Al-Hijr states that the Qur'an itself is preserved (Al-Hijr 15:9).

This name gives a person both a sense of security and a sense of trust. Someone who knows they are protected takes greater care of what has been entrusted to them.

verses.text: But if you turn away, then I have already conveyed that with which I was sent to you. My Lord will give succession to a people other than you, and you will not harm Him at all. Indeed my Lord is, over all things, Guardian."
He said, "Should I entrust you with him except [under coercion] as I entrusted you with his brother before? But Allah is the best guardian, and He is the most merciful of the merciful."

38.reflection: When you worry about the people you love, remembering that you cannot control everything can bring you peace. Like Jacob, you can do your part and leave the rest to the best of guardians. At the same time, you too have been entrusted with things to protect: a secret, a promise, a relationship, a responsibility. Today, try giving one of them a little more care.
38.practice: Today, consciously honor a promise, a confidence or a responsibility someone has entrusted to you.

39.name: Al-Muqit
39.meaning: The Nourisher, who provides every creature's sustenance, sustains its strength and watches over it.
39.description:
Al-Muqit shares its root (q-w-t) with qut, meaning food or sustenance. The name carries the sense of the One who gives every living being the nourishment its body and soul need, and who also watches over and maintains all things by His power.

Al-Muqit appears only once in the Qur'an, in Surah An-Nisa, where Sahih International renders it as "a Keeper" over all things, highlighting its sense of guarding and sustaining. Surah Hud adds that there is no creature on earth whose provision does not rest with Allah.

This name reminds us of the source of all sustenance, and of what it means to become a means of sustenance for others.

verses.text: Whoever intercedes for a good cause will have a share [i.e., reward] therefrom; and whoever intercedes for an evil cause will have a portion [i.e., burden] therefrom. And ever is Allah, over all things, a Keeper.
And there is no creature on earth but that upon Allah is its provision, and He knows its place of dwelling and place of storage. All is in a clear register.

39.reflection: Behind every bite you eat and every sip you drink are countless hands and countless efforts. Thinking that at the end of this chain there is One who watches over every creature's sustenance can change how you see your meals. You too can be a means of nourishment for others. A kind word, something shared, or a helping hand can be food for someone's day.
39.practice: Today, eat one of your meals slowly, without rushing, thinking of all the effort that brought it to your table.

40.name: Al-Hasib
40.meaning: The Reckoner, who takes full account of all things and is sufficient for His servants.
40.description:
Al-Hasib comes from the root h-s-b, which means both to count or calculate and to suffice. The word hisab, account or reckoning, comes from it. The phrase "hasbunallah" (Allah is sufficient for us) reflects the name's second meaning (Aal-Imran 3:173).

Al-Hasib appears a few times in the Qur'an. In Surah An-Nisa, believers are told to return a greeting with a better one or at least an equal one, and the verse ends: "Indeed Allah is ever, over all things, an Accountant." Even the smallest courtesy is part of the account. In Surah Al-Ahzab we read: "And sufficient is Allah as Accountant."

This name brings both responsibility and reassurance: no effort is forgotten, and He is enough for His servant.

verses.text: And when you are greeted with a greeting, greet [in return] with one better than it or [at least] return it [in a like manner]. Indeed Allah is ever, over all things, an Accountant.
[Allah praises] those who convey the messages of Allah and fear Him and do not fear anyone but Allah. And sufficient is Allah as Accountant.

40.reflection: In daily life you keep track of many things: your spending, your time, your tasks. But have you ever considered that a greeting, a smile or an act of courtesy also enters the account? This shows that even your smallest actions carry meaning. It also reminds you that you don't have to calculate everything yourself; He is enough.
40.practice: Today, answer a greeting or a kind wish with an even warmer response than the one you received.

41.name: Al-Jalil
41.meaning: The Majestic; the One whose greatness surpasses everything.
41.description:
Al-Jalil comes from the root j-l-l, which carries the ideas of greatness, loftiness and immense worth. The related word jalal describes majesty itself, and the deep reverence, mixed with awe and wonder, that such majesty stirs in the heart.

Al-Jalil is the One who is exalted in His attributes and His actions, untouched by any deficiency, and whose greatness the mind cannot fully grasp. His majesty is not meant to push people away in fear; it invites them to see everything else in its true proportion.

The name does not appear in this exact form in the Quran, but the phrase "dhul-jalali wal-ikram" (Owner of Majesty and Honor) is used twice in Surah Ar-Rahman. After reminding us that everything on earth will perish, the surah declares that only the Lord of majesty and honor remains, joining greatness and generosity in a single description.

verses.text: Everyone upon it [i.e., the earth] will perish, And there will remain the Face of your Lord, Owner of Majesty and Honor.
Blessed is the name of your Lord, Owner of Majesty and Honor.

41.reflection: Every day, things come your way that seem to make you bigger or smaller: praise, criticism, a title, a loss. All of them pass, and only His majesty remains. When you keep that in mind, you lean less on other people's approval and more on what is right. Knowing that true greatness belongs to Him protects you from arrogance and from feeling worthless alike.
41.practice: Spend a few quiet minutes today looking at the sky or a wide view, and rethink one worry of yours against that vastness.

42.name: Al-Karim
42.meaning: The Most Generous; the One whose giving asks nothing in return.
42.description:
Al-Karim comes from the root k-r-m, which gathers meanings of generosity, nobility, worth and being the finest of one's kind. In Arabic, a precious stone, fertile soil or a plant that yields abundantly can all be described as karim.

Al-Karim is the One who gives before being asked, never reminds you of His gifts, grants more than is deserved and forgives without humiliating. His generosity is not limited to material blessings; His pardon, His covering of faults and His giving of chance after chance are all part of this name.

In the Quran the name appears in a striking question in Surah Al-Infitar: what has deceived you concerning your Lord, the Generous, who created and shaped you? Surah An-Naml describes Him as "ghaniyyun karim" (Free of need and Generous), and Surah Al-Alaq calls Him "al-akram" (the Most Generous). The Quran also describes itself as "Quran karim," a noble Quran, in Surah Al-Waqi'ah.

verses.text: O mankind, what has deceived you concerning your Lord, the Generous, Who created you, proportioned you, and balanced you? In whatever form He willed has He assembled you.

42.reflection: Most of what you have, you received without ever asking: your breath, your sight, the people who love you. The Generous gave without keeping a ledger. You can show generosity too, not only with money but with your time, your attention and a kind word. When you give without expecting anything back, you will notice how much room it opens up in your own heart.
42.practice: Do one small kindness for someone today without expecting anything in return, and don't tell anyone about it.

43.name: Ar-Raqib
43.meaning: The Ever-Watchful; the One from whom nothing escapes.
43.description:
Ar-Raqib comes from the root r-q-b, meaning to watch over, to wait attentively and to guard. The related word raqabah means "neck," and it is said that the sense of watching is linked to it because someone keeping close watch stretches their neck to look.

Ar-Raqib is the One who constantly observes the states, words and intentions of His servants, watching with both knowledge and protective care. His watchfulness is not surveillance meant to oppress; it is the assurance that no good deed is lost and no wrong goes unseen.

In the Quran the name appears in the very first verse of Surah An-Nisa, in a passage about humanity's shared origin and the rights of family ties. Surah Al-Ahzab states that Allah is watchful over all things, and in Surah Al-Ma'idah Jesus acknowledges that it was Allah who was the Observer over his people.

verses.text: O mankind, fear your Lord, who created you from one soul and created from it its mate and dispersed from both of them many men and women. And fear Allah, through whom you ask one another, and the wombs. Indeed Allah is ever, over you, an Observer.

43.reflection: You are seen even in the moments you think no one is looking. That thought is not meant to frighten you; it is meant to remind you that you are never alone. The effort nobody noticed and the hurt you quietly swallowed are both known to Ar-Raqib. Living with that awareness lets your actions be shaped by inner honesty rather than by who happens to be watching.
43.practice: Do one task today that no one will see with the same care you would give it if everyone were watching.

44.name: Al-Mujib
44.meaning: The Responsive; the One who answers every call.
44.description:
Al-Mujib comes from the root j-w-b, meaning to answer, to respond to a call and to meet a need. The related word ijabah refers to accepting an invitation or responding positively to a request.

Al-Mujib is the One who hears every call directed to Him and responds in the most fitting way. He decides the form and the timing of that response, while the servant turns to Him knowing He is never far. The name tells us that His door is always open and that no sincere call goes unheard.

In the Quran the name appears in the words of the prophet Salih to his people: "qaribun mujib," near and responsive. In Surah Al-Baqarah, Allah Himself declares that when His servants ask about Him, He is near and answers the one who calls upon Him.

verses.text: And to Thamud [We sent] their brother Salih. He said, "O my people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him. He has produced you from the earth and settled you in it, so ask forgiveness of Him and then repent to Him. Indeed, my Lord is near and responsive."

And when My servants ask you, [O Muhammad], concerning Me - indeed I am near. I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me. So let them respond to Me [by obedience] and believe in Me that they may be [rightly] guided.

44.reflection: Sometimes you pray and worry that the answer is late, or that it will never come. Yet Al-Mujib hears your call the moment you make it, and knows the right shape and time of the answer better than you do. Prayer is, before any list of requests, a turning toward Him and a remembering that He is near. And when you listen to the calls of the people around you, you carry a small reflection of this name into your own life.
44.practice: Give a sincere reply today to a message or request you have been putting off.

45.name: Al-Wasi'
45.meaning: The All-Encompassing; the One whose mercy, knowledge and bounty embrace everything.
45.description:
Al-Wasi' comes from the root w-s-', which conveys vastness, abundance and the capacity to contain. Related words include wus' (capacity, means) and tawsi' (to widen or expand).

Al-Wasi' is the One whose knowledge encompasses everything, whose mercy and bounty cannot be confined, and whose treasures never diminish no matter how much He gives. His vastness is not a matter of physical space; it is limitlessness in knowledge, generosity, forgiveness and the room He gives His creation.

In the Quran the name is most often paired with "Alim" (the All-Knowing). In Surah Al-Baqarah it closes the reminder that the east and the west belong to Allah and that wherever you turn, He is there. In Surah Al-A'raf, Allah declares that His mercy encompasses all things, highlighting the mercy at the heart of this vastness.

verses.text: And to Allah belongs the east and the west. So wherever you [might] turn, there is the Face of Allah. Indeed, Allah is all-Encompassing and Knowing.

45.reflection: When you feel cornered, the world seems to shrink: options narrow and doors close. Remembering Al-Wasi' means knowing that the limits you see are not His limits. That awareness guards you against despair, and also against narrow-mindedness toward others. As your heart widens, you will find it has more room for other people's mistakes too.
45.practice: Today, listen to an opinion you disagree with all the way to the end before responding.

46.name: Al-Hakim
46.meaning: The All-Wise; the One whose every decree and creation is perfectly placed.
46.description:
Al-Hakim comes from the root h-k-m, whose basic meaning is to restrain something in order to prevent corruption, and to make something firm and sound. The words hukm (judgment), hikmah (wisdom) and muhkam (well-established) all share this root, and all of them carry the sense of rightness, soundness and sound judgment.

Al-Hakim is the One who creates everything in its proper place and measure, whose commands and prohibitions serve a purpose and a benefit, and in whose works there is nothing random. People often cannot see the wisdom in events right away; this name reminds us that order and meaning are present even where we cannot see them.

The name appears very frequently in the Quran, usually paired with "Aziz" (the Almighty) or "Alim" (the All-Knowing). In Surah Al-Baqarah, the angels confess that they know only what Allah has taught them, and they praise Him as the Knowing, the Wise.

verses.text: They said, "Exalted are You; we have no knowledge except what You have taught us. Indeed, it is You who is the Knowing, the Wise."

46.reflection: A day that didn't go to plan, a door that wouldn't open, a result that keeps getting delayed can all leave you disappointed. Remembering Al-Hakim means accepting that you don't have to understand the reason for everything right away. You can do your best and trust that the outcome, too, has its measure. Wisdom is also about you making your own decisions without haste, and putting things in their proper place.
46.practice: Before making one decision today, write down its possible outcomes on paper and think them over for a few minutes.

47.name: Al-Wadud
47.meaning: The Loving; the One who loves His servants and is most worthy of love.
47.description:
Al-Wadud comes from the root w-d-d, which carries the meanings of love, affection and wholehearted desire. The words wudd and mawaddah describe a love that does not stay hidden inside but shows itself in action.

Al-Wadud is the One who loves His servants, wishes good for them and welcomes with love those who turn to Him; the name also means the One most deserving of love. It shows that the relationship between the Creator and His servant is not only one of command and obedience, but also a bond of love.

The name appears twice in the Quran: in Surah Hud, in the words of the prophet Shu'ayb, alongside "Rahim" (the Merciful), and in Surah Al-Buruj alongside "Ghafur" (the Forgiving). Being paired with mercy and forgiveness suggests that this love embraces pardon and compassion. Surah Maryam also tells us that the Most Merciful will create affection for those who believe and do righteous deeds.

verses.text: And He is the Forgiving, the Affectionate, …

47.reflection: You often tie love to something in return: you love those who love you. Al-Wadud knows you along with your flaws and still waits for you to turn back to Him. Remembering that love helps you look at yourself more gently, too. Love gains its meaning when it is shown, not just spoken, and today you can turn it into an action.
47.practice: Reach out today to someone you love but haven't contacted in a while, simply to tell them you were thinking of them.

48.name: Al-Majid
48.meaning: The Glorious; the One whose honor and generosity are without limit.
48.description:
Al-Majid comes from the root m-j-d, which expresses glory, honor and exaltedness together with abundant generosity. It is reported that the word was also used in the sense of plenty, so the root holds both loftiness and generous abundance at once.

Al-Majid is the One whose essence is exalted, whose deeds are beautiful and whose gifts and kindness overflow. His glory comes not from greatness alone, but from greatness joined with generosity and goodness.

In the Quran the name appears in Surah Hud, when the angels bring glad tidings to the household of Abraham and describe Allah as "hamidun majid," Praiseworthy and Honorable. Surah Al-Buruj mentions Him as the glorious Owner of the Throne, and in Surahs Qaf and Al-Buruj the Quran itself is called "Quran majid," the glorious Quran.

verses.text: They said, "Are you amazed at the decree of Allah? May the mercy of Allah and His blessings be upon you, people of the house. Indeed, He is Praiseworthy and Honorable."

48.reflection: Honor is often measured by position, lineage or title. The glory of Al-Majid, however, is inseparable from His generosity; real worth shows up less in what you have than in what you do with it. You can build your own standing through the good you bring to others. Protecting someone else's dignity is one of the finest ways to protect your own.
48.practice: Sincerely appreciate someone's effort today in a setting where they can hear it.

49.name: Al-Ba'ith
49.meaning: The Resurrector; the One who raises the dead and sends forth messengers.
49.description:
Al-Ba'ith comes from the root b-'-th, which means to send, to set in motion, to awaken and to raise up. The word ba'th refers especially to resurrection after death.

Al-Ba'ith is the One who will raise people from their graves on the Day of Resurrection and who sent messengers to guide humanity. The name reminds us that life does not end with death, and that everything will be gathered again with meaning and accountability.

The name does not appear in this exact form in the Quran, but verbs from the same root occur often. Surah Al-Hajj declares that the Hour is certainly coming and that Allah will resurrect those in the graves. Surah Al-Jumu'ah uses the same root to say that it is He who sent a messenger from among the unlettered people.

verses.text: And [that they may know] that the Hour is coming - no doubt about it - and that Allah will resurrect those in the graves.

49.reflection: Waking up each morning is a small new beginning. Remembering Al-Ba'ith means knowing that your life draws its meaning not from an ending but from what continues beyond it. That awareness gives more weight to what you do today. You can bring to life a kindness you have postponed, or an intention that has been sleeping inside you.
49.practice: Take the first step today on a small task you have been putting off for a long time.

50.name: Ash-Shahid
50.meaning: The Witness; the One from whom nothing is hidden.
50.description:
Ash-Shahid comes from the root sh-h-d, meaning to be present, to see, to know and to bear witness. The words shahadah (testimony) and mushahadah (observation) share this root.

Ash-Shahid is the One who personally witnesses every event and every state, in both its visible and hidden aspects. His witnessing does not rely on reports; it is direct knowledge. The name is both a reassurance and a responsibility: it tells the wronged that their right will not be lost, and tells the wrongdoer that nothing will stay hidden.

The name appears in many verses declaring that Allah is a Witness over all things. In Surah Fussilat, after the promise that His signs will be shown on the horizons and within people themselves, the verse asks whether it is not enough that your Lord is Witness over everything.
