Surah An-Nisa likewise affirms that Allah is sufficient as a Witness.

verses.text: We will show them Our signs in the horizons and within themselves until it becomes clear to them that it is the truth. But is it not sufficient concerning your Lord that He is, over all things, a Witness?

50.reflection: Sometimes your good intentions are misunderstood, your efforts go unseen, and you feel you have to explain yourself. Knowing that Ash-Shahid witnesses everything frees you from the burden of proving yourself to everyone. The same awareness helps you stand by your word even when no one is watching. And you, too, can find the courage to speak the truth you have seen, even when it doesn't serve you.
50.practice: In one conversation today, say the truth you see, kindly but clearly, even if it doesn't work in your favor.

51.name: Al-Haqq
51.meaning: The Truth; the One whose existence is real and unchanging.
51.description:
Al-Haqq comes from the root h-q-q, meaning to be firmly established, to come true, and to be right and fitting. In Arabic, haqq means both what is true and what is rightfully due to someone; the word haqiqah (reality) comes from the same root.

Al-Haqq is the One whose existence depends on nothing else, whose being is certain and unchanging. His word is true, His promise is real and His judgment is just. Everything other than Him owes its existence to Him, which makes Him the source of all truth.

In Surah Al-Hajj the Quran states that Allah is the True Reality, that He gives life to the dead and that He has power over all things. The same emphasis returns in another verse of Surah Al-Hajj and in Surah Luqman, contrasting Him with the falsehood of whatever is worshipped besides Him. In Surah An-Nur He is called "al-haqq al-mubin," the manifest Truth.

verses.text: That is because Allah is the True Reality and because He gives life to the dead and because He is over all things competent…

51.reflection: Small lies, exaggerations and half-truths can look like an easy way out during the day. Remembering Al-Haqq means knowing that solid ground can only be built on what is true. When you hold on to the truth, you never need another lie to protect it. Honesty can feel hard at times, but it leaves you lighter inside.
51.practice: In your conversations today, take care to describe things exactly as they are, without exaggeration.

52.name: Al-Wakil
52.meaning: The Trustee; the One upon whom one relies and who best manages all affairs.
52.description:
Al-Wakil comes from the root w-k-l, meaning to entrust a matter to someone, to rely on them and to lean on them. The word tawakkul, placing one's trust in someone and handing over one's affairs to them, shares this root.

Al-Wakil is the One who takes charge of the affairs of those who rely on Him, manages them in the best way and is sufficient for them. Unlike human agents, His care is free of any shortcoming, fatigue or neglect. Trust in Him does not mean abandoning effort; it means doing what you can and then leaving the outcome to Him with confidence.

The name appears in several verses affirming that Allah is sufficient as a Trustee. Surah Aal-Imran describes believers who were told that an army had gathered against them, yet the threat only increased their faith, and they said, "Sufficient for us is Allah, and He is the best Disposer of affairs."

verses.text: Those to whom people [i.e., hypocrites] said, "Indeed, the people have gathered against you, so fear them." But it [merely] increased them in faith, and they said, "Sufficient for us is Allah, and [He is] the best Disposer of affairs."

52.reflection: When you face something you cannot control, your mind keeps spinning scenarios and wears you out. Remembering Al-Wakil means learning to do what you can and then let the rest go. This is not escaping responsibility; it is handing the part you cannot carry to the right place. That way, your energy goes into the next step you can actually take, not into worry.
52.practice: Pick one thing that is worrying you today, identify a single step you can take on it, take that step and let the rest go.

53.name: Al-Qawiyy
53.meaning: The All-Strong; the One whose power is complete and never fails.
53.description:
Al-Qawiyy comes from the root q-w-y, meaning to be strong, to be capable of a task and to endure. The words quwwah (strength) and taqwiyah (reinforcement) come from the same root.

Al-Qawiyy is the One whose power is perfect, whom no task can strain and whose strength never diminishes. His power is never arbitrary; it works together with kindness, justice and wisdom. The name is a refuge for those who feel powerless and a measure, even a warning, for those who hold power.

In the Quran the name is most often paired with "Aziz" (the Exalted in Might). In Surah Ash-Shura, after reminding us that Allah is Subtle with His servants and provides for whom He wills, the verse closes with these two names. The same pairing appears in Surahs Al-Hajj, Al-Hadid and Al-Mujadilah.

verses.text: Allah is Subtle with His servants; He gives provision to whom He wills. And He is the Powerful, the Exalted in Might.

53.reflection: In hard times you feel the limits of your own strength very clearly. Remembering Al-Qawiyy means knowing that you are not the true source of strength, and finding relief in that. It also reminds you that whatever strength you have been given is a trust, meant to protect the weak rather than overpower them. Sometimes being strong simply means standing patiently in the quietest moment.
53.practice: Lend a hand today to someone who is having a harder time than you.

54.name: Al-Matin
54.meaning: The Firm; the One whose strength is unshakable and unceasing.
54.description:
Al-Matin comes from the root m-t-n, which conveys firmness, solidity and endurance. In Arabic, matn refers to the back and to the strong, load-bearing part of something, the part that holds everything else up.

Al-Matin is the One whose strength is utterly firm, never touched by fatigue, weakening or interruption. Where Al-Qawiyy speaks of the completeness of His power, Al-Matin highlights its constancy and steadfastness.

As a name, it appears in Surah Adh-Dhariyat, in the verse declaring that Allah is the Provider and the firm possessor of strength. The verse comes right after the verses describing the purpose for which humans were created, and reminds us that He is the true source of all provision. The same root is used in Surahs Al-A'raf and Al-Qalam to describe the firmness of His plan.

verses.text: Indeed, it is Allah who is the [continual] Provider, the firm possessor of strength.

54.reflection: Even life's small shocks can shake your resolve. Remembering Al-Matin means knowing that what you lean on is firm, and trying to take a share of that steadiness. Steadfastness is not never being shaken; it is getting back up after you are. The consistency you show in a habit or a promise can be a small reflection of this name in your life.
54.practice: Keep one small promise you made to yourself today, even if you don't feel like it.

55.name: Al-Waliyy
55.meaning: The Protecting Friend; the Ally and Guardian of those who believe.
55.description:
Al-Waliyy comes from the root w-l-y, meaning to be near, to follow closely with nothing in between, to befriend and to take charge of a matter. The words wilayah (guardianship) and tawalli (taking charge, turning toward) share this root.

Al-Waliyy is the Friend of those who believe, the One who helps them, takes charge of their affairs and protects them. This friendship is not a relationship between equals; it is the All-Powerful showing closeness and care to the servant who turns to Him.

The name appears in many verses. Surah Al-Baqarah tells us that Allah is the ally of those who believe and brings them out of darkness into light. In Surah Ash-Shura, He is described as the One who sends down rain after people had despaired and spreads His mercy, and is named together as "Waliyy" and "Hamid."

verses.text: And it is He who sends down the rain after they had despaired and spreads His mercy. And He is the Protector, the Praiseworthy.

55.reflection: Like rain falling just when you thought hope had run dry, help sometimes comes from where you least expect it. Remembering Al-Waliyy means knowing that you do not walk the road alone. Someone aware of that friendship learns how to be a friend to others as well. Today, you can be a quiet friend in someone's life who helps carry their load.
55.practice: Ask someone you know is going through a hard time whether there is anything they need today.

56.name: Al-Hamid
56.meaning: The Praiseworthy; the One deserving of all praise.
56.description:
Al-Hamid comes from the root h-m-d, meaning to praise someone and extol them for their fine qualities and good deeds. The word hamd includes both gratitude for a blessing and praise of what is beautiful for its own sake.

Al-Hamid is the One worthy of praise in His essence, His attributes and His actions. He deserves praise whether or not anyone offers it; He has no need of His servants' praise, and it is the one who praises who gains. The fact that the opening chapter of the Quran begins with praise shows how central this meaning is.

In the Quran the name is frequently paired with "Ghani" (the Free of need). Surah Fatir reminds humanity that they are the ones in need of Allah, while Allah is Free of need and Praiseworthy. The same pairing appears in Surahs Luqman and Ibrahim.

verses.text: O mankind, you are those in need of Allah, while Allah is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy.

56.reflection: On most days, criticizing comes more easily than praising. Remembering Al-Hamid means learning to notice the good around you and to see where it truly comes from. Praising Him matters not because He needs it, but because it brings light to your own heart. Giving thanks for every good thing you notice changes the way you see.
56.practice: Before evening, write down a few good things you came across today and give thanks for each one.

57.name: Al-Muhsi
57.meaning: The Reckoner; the One who knows the number, measure and detail of everything.
57.description:
Al-Muhsi comes from the root h-s-y. The related word hasa means "pebble," and it is said that because the Arabs once used pebbles to keep count, the word ihsa' came to mean counting, recording one by one and fully encompassing.

Al-Muhsi is the One who knows everything by its number, measure and detail, missing not a single leaf, drop, breath or deed. His knowledge is never approximate; it is complete. The name reminds us that no good or bad deed, however small it seems, is ever lost.

The name does not appear in this exact form in the Quran, but verbs from the same root occur in many verses. Surah Maryam states that He has enumerated everyone and counted them precisely. Surah Al-Jinn says that He has counted all things in number, and Surah Ya-Sin tells us that everything has been recorded in a clear register.

verses.text: He has enumerated them and counted them a [full] counting.

57.reflection: Sometimes you think the small good things you do don't matter, that no one notices them. Al-Muhsi overlooks nothing; a single kind word, a single moment of patience, is within His knowledge. That awareness keeps you from belittling small kindnesses and from taking small mistakes lightly. Caring about the details of your life is a way of respecting it.
57.practice: This evening, take a few minutes to look back over the blessings you received and the small kindnesses you did today.

58.name: Al-Mubdi'
58.meaning: The Originator; the One who brings creation into being for the first time, without precedent.
58.description:
Al-Mubdi' comes from the root b-d-', meaning to begin, to do something for the first time and to bring it forth. The words ibtida' (beginning) and mabda' (starting point) come from the same root.

Al-Mubdi' is the One who brings things into existence for the first time, when no model existed before, and who initiates creation. Every newborn creature, every sprouting seed and every new day can be seen as a sign of this originating power. The name is usually mentioned together with Al-Mu'id, the One who restores creation.

The name does not appear in this exact form in the Quran, but verbs from the same root occur in many verses. Surah Al-Buruj states briefly and decisively that it is He who originates creation and then repeats it. Surahs Yunus, Ar-Rum and Al-Ankabut also point to the first creation as evidence of the resurrection.

verses.text: Indeed, it is He who originates [creation] and repeats.

58.reflection: Starting something new is often the hardest step; you hesitate and wait for the right moment. Remembering Al-Mubdi' means seeing that every beginning ultimately rests on His creating. When you think of the One who brought everything into being from nothing, you realize your own small beginnings are not worthless either. Rather than waiting for perfect conditions, you can start something good today.
58.practice: Start a good habit you have long wanted to build by giving it just a few minutes today.

59.name: Al-Mu'id
59.meaning: The Restorer; the One who brings creation back into being after it has passed away.
59.description:
Al-Mu'id comes from the root '-w-d, meaning to return, to come back and to repeat something. Words such as i'adah (restoration), 'adah (habit) and 'id (a festival that returns each year) share this root, and all carry the sense of return and repetition.

Al-Mu'id is the One who brings His creation back to life after death and repeats the creation He began. The Quran stresses that the One who created the first time is able to create again, and that this is even easier for Him. The cycle of the seasons and the life that begins anew each morning can be seen as signs of this name.

The name does not appear in this exact form in the Quran, but verbs from the same root appear often, usually alongside verbs of origination. Surah Ar-Rum declares that it is He who begins creation and then repeats it. Surahs Al-Buruj and Yunus also mention originating and repeating together.

verses.text: And it is He who begins creation; then He repeats it, and that is [even] easier for Him. To Him belongs the highest description [i.e., attribute] in the heavens and earth. And He is the Exalted in Might, the Wise.

59.reflection: Something you lost, a relationship that broke down or a task left unfinished can look like an ending with no way back. Remembering Al-Mu'id means knowing that returning and starting over are always possible. Turning back from a mistake, apologizing or trying again are all reflections of this name in your life. Trying something again is not defeat; it is a sign of patience and hope.
59.practice: Take one small step today toward a relationship that has grown distant, even if it is just a short message.

60.name: Al-Muhyi
60.meaning: The Giver of Life; the One who revives the dead and brings dead earth back to life.
60.description:
Al-Muhyi comes from the root h-y-y, meaning to live, to be alive and to come to life. The words hayah (life), ihya' (revival) and Hayy (the Ever-Living) share this root.

Al-Muhyi is the One who gives life to living beings, revives the dead and brings parched earth back to life with rain. This giving of life is not limited to the body; the Quran also describes guidance and faith as a kind of coming to life. Together with Al-Mumit, the name shows that life and death belong to Him alone.

In the Quran the name appears in Surahs Ar-Rum and Fussilat as "muhyi al-mawta," the Giver of life to the dead. In Surah Ar-Rum, we are invited to look at the earth revived by rain and reminded that the One who brings the land back to life will also raise the dead. In this way, every spring becomes a visible sign of the resurrection.

verses.text: So observe the effects of the mercy of Allah - how He gives life to the earth after its lifelessness. Indeed, that [same one] will give life to the dead, and He is over all things competent.

60.reflection: Have you ever watched dry soil turn green after the first rain? Remembering Al-Muhyi means knowing that what seems dead can come back to life: a hope, a relationship, an enthusiasm inside you. With your words and your attention, you can bring life to someone's day. Noticing the life around you awakens the life within you as well.
60.practice: Water a plant today, or spend a few minutes outside simply paying attention to the living things around you.

61.name: Al-Mumit
61.meaning: The One who creates death and brings life to its appointed end.
61.description:
Al-Mumit comes from the root m-w-t, "to die," and means the One who causes death and who created death itself. It is usually understood alongside Al-Muhyi, the Giver of Life: the One who grants life is also the One who sets its limit.

The Qur'an does not present death as mere extinction but as something created with purpose. Surah Al-Mulk states that death and life were created so that people might show which of them is best in deed. Seen this way, death is a reality that gives life its weight and meaning.

The form Al-Mumit does not itself appear in the Qur'an, but many verses describe God as the One who "gives life and causes death." The second verse of Surah Al-Hadid is one of them.

verses.text: [He] who created death and life to test you [as to] which of you is best in deed - and He is the Exalted in Might, the Forgiving - …
His is the dominion of the heavens and earth. He gives life and causes death, and He is over all things competent.

61.reflection: Remembering death does not make life smaller; it makes each day more precious. Knowing that your time has a limit helps you bring the good things you keep postponing into today. Making peace with someone, telling the people you love that you love them, finishing a kindness you left half done: the best moment for these is usually now. This Name invites you not to fear, but to live more awake and more gently.
61.practice: Today, send a short message with a thank-you or an apology you have been putting off for a long time.

62.name: Al-Hayy
62.meaning: The Ever-Living, whose life has no beginning, no end, and no source outside Himself.
62.description:
Al-Hayy comes from the root h-y-y, "to live, to be alive." God's life is not like created life, which begins, depends on causes, and eventually ends. His life is His own, without beginning or end.

All life in every living thing is a gift from Him. Knowledge, will and power all presuppose life, which is why Al-Hayy is often seen as the foundation of many other Names.

In the Qur'an, Al-Hayy appears alongside Al-Qayyum in the Verse of the Throne (Al-Baqarah 2:255), in Aal-Imran 3:2 and in Ta-Ha 20:111. Surah Al-Furqan calls believers to rely on "the Ever-Living who does not die," and Surah Ghafir declares, "He is the Ever-Living."

verses.text: And rely upon the Ever-Living who does not die, and exalt [Allah] with His praise. And sufficient is He to be, with the sins of His servants, [fully] Aware - …
He is the Ever-Living; there is no deity except Him, so call upon Him, [being] sincere to Him in religion. [All] praise is [due] to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

62.reflection: Everything around you changes, grows tired and eventually ends: people, plans, opportunities. When you place all your trust in what is passing, you are shaken whenever it is shaken. Al-Hayy reminds you that you can lean on a Life that never runs out. That support also awakens the life within you, calling you to live the days you are given with attention and care.
62.practice: Today, spend five minutes outside looking closely at a tree or a plant, and try to notice the life in it.

63.name: Al-Qayyum
63.meaning: The Self-Sustaining, who holds up and watches over all that exists.
63.description:
Al-Qayyum is an intensive form from the root q-w-m, "to stand, to take charge of something." It carries two meanings at once: the One who needs nothing in order to exist, and the One who keeps everything else standing, protecting and managing it.

The order of the universe cannot carry on by itself for even a moment; the preservation of the heavens and the earth and the continued existence of every creature depend on His care. The Verse of the Throne says that neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him, expressing that this care never pauses.

Al-Qayyum appears three times in the Qur'an (Al-Baqarah 2:255, Aal-Imran 3:2, Ta-Ha 20:111), and each time it is paired with Al-Hayy, highlighting the link between being ever-living and upholding all things.

verses.text: Allah - there is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living, the Self-Sustaining.
And [all] faces will be humbled before the Ever-Living, the Self-Sustaining. And he will have failed who carries injustice.

63.reflection: Sometimes you feel as if you have to hold everything up on your own: work, family, relationships, the future. Yet you are not the true support of anything; you are responsible only for your part. Seeing this does not make you careless; it lifts weight you were never meant to carry. Do what you can, then taste the calm of leaving the rest to the One who sustains all things.
63.practice: Today, write down the responsibility that weighs on you most, add one step that is actually in your hands, and take only that step.

64.name: Al-Wajid
64.meaning: The Finder, who lacks nothing and finds whatever He wills.
64.description:
Al-Wajid comes from the root w-j-d, "to find, to obtain." It expresses that God never loses anything, that whatever He wills is present with Him, and that He is never in a state of lack or want.

The Name also carries a sense of richness and sufficiency. People can lose things and fail to find what they seek; God is never deprived of what He wills. Some scholars explained this Name as close in meaning to Al-Ghani, the Self-Sufficient.

Al-Wajid does not appear in this form in the Qur'an; it is included in the list of Beautiful Names transmitted in hadith. Its root, however, is common in the Qur'an. Surah Ad-Duha reminds the Prophet how God "found" him an orphan, lost and in need, and gave him refuge, guidance and sufficiency.

verses.text: Did He not find you an orphan and give [you] refuge? And He found you lost and guided [you], And He found you poor and made [you] self-sufficient.

64.reflection: At times you may feel lost, incomplete or alone. The verses of Surah Ad-Duha remind you that even in the hardest seasons you are seen and found. Remembering how a way opened for you before can help you face today with hope. You, too, can notice someone around you who feels lost and become a small sign for them.
64.practice: Today, write three sentences about a situation that once seemed to have no way out, and how a way opened for you.

65.name: Al-Maajid
65.meaning: The Glorious, whose honor is exalted and whose generosity is abundant.
65.description:
Al-Maajid comes from the root m-j-d, "to excel in honor and nobility, to be vast in generosity." In Arabic, the word majd joins the idea of glory with that of abundant, open-handed giving.

The Name describes God as exalted in His essence and His acts, with that exaltedness showing itself as generosity toward His servants. The One whose glory is highest reveals His greatness through giving.

The form Al-Maajid does not occur in the Qur'an, but Al-Majid, from the same root and very close in meaning, does. Surah Al-Buruj calls Him the "Honorable Owner of the Throne," and in Surah Hud the angels tell the household of Abraham that He is "Praiseworthy and Honorable."

verses.text: And He is the Forgiving, the Affectionate, Honorable Owner of the Throne, …
They said, "Are you amazed at the decree of Allah? May the mercy of Allah and His blessings be upon you, people of the house. Indeed, He is Praiseworthy and Honorable."

65.reflection: True honor is not found in keeping what you have to yourself, but in being able to give from it. Whether your means are great or small, the way you share them shapes your character. Remember that generosity is not only material: your time, your attention and a kind word are gifts too. Letting someone feel valued today can be a small reflection of this glory.
65.practice: Today, offer someone a small kindness without expecting anything back, such as buying them a tea or giving them your unhurried time.

66.name: Al-Wahid
66.meaning: The One, unique in His essence, attributes and acts.
66.description:
Al-Wahid comes from the root w-h-d, "to be one, to be single." God's oneness is more than being one in number: it means He has no partner and no likeness in His essence, His attributes or His acts.

The word tawhid, the affirmation of God's oneness, comes from the same root. It is the foundation of Islamic belief: recognizing that despite the multitude of things, everything depends on a single Creator. That recognition also gathers a scattered heart in one direction.

In the Qur'an, Al-Wahid appears in many places, most often paired with Al-Qahhar (for example, Ar-Ra'd 13:16). In Surah Al-Baqarah, "your god is one God" is stated together with the Names Ar-Rahman and Ar-Rahim.

verses.text: And your god is one God. There is no deity [worthy of worship] except Him, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

66.reflection: Throughout the day, many things pull your attention in different directions: expectations, worries, other people's approval. When you are tied to so many centers, it is natural to feel scattered inside. Al-Wahid reminds you that when you turn toward one center, your heart gathers itself too. Today, try to keep the intention behind what you do simple and sincere.
66.practice: Today, set aside twenty minutes to focus on a single task and leave your phone in another room while you do.

67.name: Al-Ahad
67.meaning: The Absolutely One, indivisible and without equal.
67.description:
Al-Ahad shares the root w-h-d with Al-Wahid. Scholars have drawn a subtle distinction between the two: Al-Wahid stresses that God has no partner, while Al-Ahad stresses an absolute oneness that admits no division within and no comparison with anything else.

This Name sets a boundary against the mind's tendency to picture God in the image of created things. He fits no mold; He neither begets nor is born, and nothing is equal to Him.

As a Name of God, Al-Ahad appears in the first verse of Surah Al-Ikhlas. Though very short, this surah expresses the essence of God's oneness in the simplest possible terms.

verses.text: Say, "He is Allah, [who is] One, Allah, the Eternal Refuge. He neither begets nor is born, Nor is there to Him any equivalent."

67.reflection: No one can fully take your place, and you are no one's copy; uniqueness is woven throughout creation. When you keep measuring yourself against others, you miss what is truly yours. Al-Ahad reminds you that turning toward the One beyond all comparison can free you from the fatigue of comparing. Today, let yourself walk your own path at your own pace.
67.practice: Today, the first time you catch yourself comparing your life with someone else's, pause and recall one blessing in your own.

68.name: As-Samad
68.meaning: The Eternal Refuge, who needs nothing while everything needs Him.
68.description:
As-Samad comes from the root s-m-d. The word describes a master to whom people turn in times of need; it also carries the sense of something solid and complete, lacking nothing.

These two meanings complete each other: God needs nothing, and everything needs Him. Surah Fatir puts it plainly: people are in need of God, while He is free of all need.

As-Samad appears only once in the Qur'an, in the second verse of Surah Al-Ikhlas. Despite that single mention, it is regarded as one of the most comprehensive Names describing God.

verses.text: Allah, the Eternal Refuge.
O mankind, you are those in need of Allah, while Allah is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy.

68.reflection: For every need, you turn to some door: a person, an institution, a resource. These are means, but none of them is a true refuge; each depends on something else. As-Samad teaches you to free your heart from that long chain of dependence and anchor it in the One who needs nothing. That anchor brings balance to what you expect from others and leaves you freer.
68.practice: Today, notice a small need of someone around you and meet it without expecting anything in return.

69.name: Al-Qadir
69.meaning: The All-Able, who has power to do whatever He wills.
69.description:
Al-Qadir comes from the root q-d-r, "to be able, to measure and determine." Power, for God, means doing what He wills without any obstacle; His power has no limit and He is never unable.

The root's sense of "measure" adds depth to this Name: God's power is not random but measured and wise. Everything is created with a precise proportion and order.

The Qur'an frequently speaks of God's power with the phrase "He is over all things competent." Surah Ya-Sin reminds us that the One who created the heavens and the earth is surely able to create their like, inviting reflection on the resurrection.

verses.text: Is not He who created the heavens and the earth Able to create the likes of them? Yes, [it is so]; and He is the Knowing Creator.

69.reflection: Some situations may leave you feeling completely helpless. Having limited strength is part of being human; accepting that limit is not weakness but honesty. Al-Qadir reminds you that where your strength ends, everything does not end. That trust keeps you from dismissing the small step you can take and helps you hold on to hope.
69.practice: Today, choose something that feels impossible, identify the smallest step you could take toward it, and take that step right away.

70.name: Al-Muqtadir
70.meaning: The All-Powerful, whose power is complete and fully exercised.
70.description:
Al-Muqtadir shares the root q-d-r with Al-Qadir, but its verbal form intensifies the meaning. It expresses power that is uninterrupted, flawless and actively at work in every situation.

Al-Qadir emphasizes that the power exists; Al-Muqtadir emphasizes that it is carried out with complete command over all things. No task burdens Him, and nothing can hinder what He decrees.

In the Qur'an, this Name appears in a verse of Surah Al-Kahf describing how fleeting worldly life is, and in Surah Al-Qamar, which says the righteous will be seated "near a Sovereign, Perfect in Ability."

verses.text: Indeed, the righteous will be among gardens and rivers, In a seat of honor near a Sovereign, Perfect in Ability.

And present to them the example of the life of this world, [its being] like rain which We send down from the sky, and the vegetation of the earth mingles with it and [then] it becomes dry remnants, scattered by the winds. And Allah is ever, over all things, Perfect in Ability.

70.reflection: Worldly life flourishes and then withers, like the parable in Surah Al-Kahf; much of what you think of as power is just as temporary. Titles, resources and the feeling of control can all change. Al-Muqtadir reminds you where real and lasting power lies, guarding you from both arrogance and despair. Whatever power you hold, large or small, take care to use it with justice and mercy.
70.practice: Today, speak patiently and without raising your voice to someone who depends on you, such as a colleague or a child.

71.name: Al-Muqaddim
71.meaning: The Expediter, who brings forward whatever He wills according to His wisdom.
71.description:
Al-Muqaddim comes from the root q-d-m, "to be in front, to go ahead," and means the One who brings forward and advances. He determines what comes first in time, rank or degree.

This Name is paired with Al-Mu'akhkhir. That some people stand out in certain ways while others advance in different areas is part of an order He has set with wisdom; these differences are both a test and a way for people to complete one another.

Al-Muqaddim does not appear as an attribute in the Qur'an; it is found in hadith and in the lists of Beautiful Names. Its meaning, however, is clear in verses stating that some people have been favored over others, and that both those who came before and those who come after are known to God.

verses.text: Look how We have favored [in provision] some of them over others. But the Hereafter is greater in degrees [of difference] and greater in distinction.
And We have already known the preceding [generations] among you, and We have already known the later [ones to come].

71.reflection: When you see others reach a place before you, you may feel a quiet unease. Yet each person has a different field and a different time in which they come forward; there is a path and a time set for you too. Al-Muqaddim invites you to let go of envy and look at your own priorities. Deciding what truly deserves to come first in your life can be an everyday reflection of this Name.
71.practice: Today, move the most important task you keep postponing to the top of your list and do it first.

72.name: Al-Mu'akhkhir
72.meaning: The Delayer, who holds back whatever He wills according to His wisdom.
72.description:
Al-Mu'akhkhir comes from the root '-kh-r, "to be behind, to come later," and means the One who defers and holds back. He determines what is left for later and when the time for each thing arrives.

God's delay is often a mercy and an opportunity: people are given time to reflect, to turn back and to set right their mistakes. Yet once the appointed time comes, it is not postponed, which reminds us how valuable time is.

Al-Mu'akhkhir does not appear as an attribute in the Qur'an; it is mentioned in hadith together with Al-Muqaddim. In Surah Nuh, the Prophet Noah tells his people that God will delay them for a specified term, but that when His appointed time comes, it will not be delayed.

verses.text: To worship Allah, fear Him and obey me. He [i.e., Allah] will forgive you of your sins and delay you for a specified term. Indeed, the time [set by] Allah, when it comes, will not be delayed, if you only knew."

72.reflection: When something you long for is delayed, impatience can set in; a door or an opportunity may not arrive when you expected it. Al-Mu'akhkhir invites you to consider that what looks like a delay may hold wisdom. The waiting can be space given to you to prepare and to grow. At the same time, remember that the time you are given is not unlimited, and use it well.
72.practice: Today, for something whose delay frustrates you, write down one idea for how you could make good use of the waiting.

73.name: Al-Awwal
73.meaning: The First, whose existence has no beginning and who precedes all things.
73.description:
Al-Awwal means "the First, the One who comes before." God's existence has no beginning; He is before everything and brings everything into being. Nothing existed before Him.

This Name points to the source of all existence: He is the One who begins creation. Every beginning, every first step and every new day is possible through His creating. Even when a person starts something, they move within an order He has established.

Al-Awwal appears in the third verse of Surah Al-Hadid together with Al-Akhir, Az-Zahir and Al-Batin. Taken together, these four Names describe God's absoluteness, encompassing time and all that exists.

verses.text: He is the First and the Last, the Ascendant and the Intimate, and He is, of all things, Knowing.

And it is He who begins creation; then He repeats it, and that is [even] easier for Him. To Him belongs the highest description [i.e., attribute] in the heavens and earth. And He is the Exalted in Might, the Wise.

73.reflection: Everything in your life has a beginning: a relationship, a habit, a journey. Directing your intention to the First when you begin something gives it firm ground. Al-Awwal asks you what you have placed first in your heart. The first thought you carry into your day can set the tone for everything that follows.
73.practice: Today, begin your first task by reminding yourself in one sentence why you are doing it.

74.name: Al-Akhir
74.meaning: The Last, whose existence has no end and who remains after all things pass.
74.description:
Al-Akhir comes from the root '-kh-r, "the last, what comes after," the same root as Al-Mu'akhkhir. God's existence has no end; when everything else has passed away, He remains.

This Name reminds us that everything in the world is temporary and only He endures. Surah Ar-Rahman states that everyone on the earth will perish, and only the Face of your Lord, Owner of Majesty and Honor, will remain. This truth calls a person not to despair, but to turn toward what lasts.

Al-Akhir appears in the third verse of Surah Al-Hadid alongside Al-Awwal. A Being without beginning or end offers lasting support to people who live within time.

verses.text: He is the First and the Last, the Ascendant and the Intimate, and He is, of all things, Knowing.
Everyone upon it [i.e., the earth] will perish, And there will remain the Face of your Lord, Owner of Majesty and Honor.

74.reflection: Seeing something end can sadden you: a season of life, a companionship, an opportunity. Al-Akhir reminds you that behind every ending there is One who never ends. This does not deny the pain of loss; it gives that pain meaning and consolation. Try to direct your effort and your love toward things that leave a lasting trace.
74.practice: Today, do a small good whose benefit will outlast you, such as teaching someone a skill you know.

75.name: Az-Zahir
75.meaning: The Manifest, whose existence is evident through His signs and who is above all things.
75.description:
Az-Zahir comes from the root z-h-r, "to appear, to become visible; to prevail." Though God is not seen with the eyes, His existence is evident through His works and signs, and He holds supremacy over all things.

The order of the universe, the balance within living beings and the inner world of the human being are all seen as signs pointing to Him. Surah Fussilat says that God will show His signs both in the horizons and within people themselves.

Az-Zahir appears in the third verse of Surah Al-Hadid together with its counterpart, Al-Batin. The pairing conveys that He is both clearly evident in everything and beyond all comprehension.

verses.text: He is the First and the Last, the Ascendant and the Intimate, and He is, of all things, Knowing.

We will show them Our signs in the horizons and within themselves until it becomes clear to them that it is the truth. But is it not sufficient concerning your Lord that He is, over all things, a Witness?

75.reflection: Each day, many things pass before your eyes unnoticed out of habit: the sunrise, a child's laughter, the flawless workings of your own body. Az-Zahir reminds you of the difference between looking and seeing. When you look with attention, what seemed ordinary begins to carry meaning. Today, open your eyes to be amazed again by what you have grown used to.
75.practice: Today, spend one minute closely examining something you see every day but never really look at, like a leaf or your own hand.

76.name: Al-Batin
76.meaning: The Hidden, beyond the grasp of mind and senses, who knows the inner reality of all things.
76.description:
Al-Batin comes from the root b-t-n, "to be hidden, to be within." The reality of God's essence cannot be grasped by the senses or the intellect, and at the same time He knows the inner side and the secret of everything.

This Name can be considered from two sides. On one hand, His reality lies beyond human comprehension; on the other, He is closer to a person than their jugular vein and knows what passes through them. Distance and nearness meet in this Name.

Al-Batin appears in the third verse of Surah Al-Hadid together with Az-Zahir. A verse in Surah Qaf expresses the nearness side of this Name in a striking way.

verses.text: He is the First and the Last, the Ascendant and the Intimate, and He is, of all things, Knowing.
And We have already created man and know what his soul whispers to him, and We are closer to him than [his] jugular vein.

76.reflection: You cannot always put into words what is happening inside you; sometimes words fall short, sometimes you fear being misunderstood. Al-Batin reminds you that even your most hidden thoughts and feelings are known, which is both a comfort and a responsibility. Staying honest where no one can see is how this Name shows up in daily life. The closer your inner world and your outward face become, the deeper the peace you find.
76.practice: Today, do a small kindness that no one will know about, and do not tell anyone.

77.name: Al-Wali
77.meaning: The Governor, who takes charge of, directs and protects all things.
77.description:
Al-Wali comes from the root w-l-y, "to be near, to take charge, to govern," and means the One who takes charge of the affairs of all beings, ordering and directing them. The Name Al-Wali in the sense of "Protecting Friend" shares the same root.

This Name expresses that nothing in the universe is left unattended; everything is under direction and care. God's governance rests on knowledge, wisdom and mercy.

Al-Wali appears in the Qur'an in the form "wal" in verse 11 of Surah Ar-Ra'd: people have no patron besides Him. The same verse states that God will not change the condition of a people until they change what is within themselves.

verses.text: For him [i.e., each one] are successive [angels] before and behind him who protect him by the decree of Allah. Indeed, Allah will not change the condition of a people until they change what is in themselves. And when Allah intends for a people ill, there is no repelling it. And there is not for them besides Him any patron.

77.reflection: In some areas of your life, responsibility rests with you: a family, a team, or simply your own daily routine. Al-Wali reminds you where true governance lies, and invites you to treat the small areas entrusted to you as a trust. The verse in Surah Ar-Ra'd says that change begins within a person. Before trying to change others, looking at something you can change in yourself is a good place to start.
77.practice: Today, in a situation you often complain about, pick one thing in your own behavior you can change and put it into practice.

78.name: Al-Muta'ali
78.meaning: The Supremely Exalted, far above every deficiency and comparison.
78.description:
Al-Muta'ali comes from the root '-l-w, "to be high, to be exalted." Its verbal form expresses the utmost degree of exaltedness: God is far above every deficiency and limitation of created things and every comparison the human mind might construct.

Sharing its root with Al-Aliyy and Al-A'la, Al-Muta'ali conveys that this exaltedness is not a matter of physical place but of rank and perfection. His exaltedness is mentioned together with His knowledge of both the hidden and the seen.

The Name appears in the ninth verse of Surah Ar-Ra'd alongside Al-Kabir: He is the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, the Grand, the Exalted.

verses.text: [He is] Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, the Grand, the Exalted.

78.reflection: Sometimes a small argument, a remark or a hurt can fill your whole mind. Al-Muta'ali reminds you to raise your gaze a little and look at events from a wider place. Reflecting on the Most High lightens the weight of what is minor and draws you away from petty calculations. Today, try looking at something that occupies you by asking how it will look a year from now.
78.practice: Today, instead of replying at once to a word that hurt you, wait a while and then respond calmly.

79.name: Al-Barr
79.meaning: The Source of All Goodness, generous and faithful toward His servants.
79.description:
Al-Barr comes from the root b-r-r, "to do good, to be true and faithful." The word brings together goodness, benevolence, keeping one's word and wide-reaching kindness.

God's goodness does not depend on whether His servants deserve it; He keeps His promises, is kind to His servants and is the One who initiates good. The word birr, used for goodness between people, comes from the same root; the phrase birr al-walidayn, kindness to parents, is one example.

Al-Barr appears in Surah At-Tur, where the people of Paradise recall that they used to call upon God before, and that He is the Beneficent, the Merciful.

verses.text: Indeed, we used to supplicate Him before. Indeed, it is He who is the Beneficent, the Merciful."

79.reflection: Most of the good you receive arrives quietly, not because you earned it but because it was given to you. Al-Barr invites you to notice this unearned goodness and reflect it to those around you. A small kindness to your parents, to people close to you or to a stranger is this Name's trace in your life. Goodness widens the heart of the one who gives it, too.
79.practice: Today, call your parents or an elder who has done a lot for you and ask how they are.

80.name: At-Tawwab
80.meaning: The Ever-Accepting of Repentance, who turns His servants toward return.
80.description:
At-Tawwab comes from the root t-w-b, "to return." Repentance is a servant's return to God after a mistake; God's "turning," in turn, is guiding the servant toward repentance and accepting that return. The intensive form At-Tawwab conveys that this acceptance happens again and again.

This Name reminds us that no mistake leaves a person at a point of no return. The door is always open; what matters is turning back with sincere regret and taking a step to make things right.

At-Tawwab appears in many verses of the Qur'an, most often paired with Ar-Rahim. The account of Adam, who received words from his Lord and whose repentance was accepted, is among the best-known illustrations of this Name.

verses.text: Then Adam received from his Lord [some] words, and He accepted his repentance. Indeed, it is He who is the Accepting of Repentance, the Merciful.
Do they not know that it is Allah who accepts repentance from His servants and receives charities and that it is Allah who is the Accepting of Repentance, the Merciful?

80.reflection: When you make a mistake, it is easy either to avoid thinking about it or to keep blaming yourself. At-Tawwab points to a third way: acknowledging the mistake, feeling genuine regret and beginning again. Knowing that the door of return is never closed to you gives you both courage and responsibility. Try to meet other people's mistakes with the same openness, giving them room to begin again.
80.practice: Today, sincerely apologize to someone you have hurt or neglected, and take one step to set things right.

81.name: Al-Muntaqim
81.meaning: The One who brings just requital for wrongdoing.
81.description:
Al-Muntaqim comes from the Arabic root n-q-m, which carries the sense of rejecting an injustice and answering a wrong. Among people the word can suggest anger or a personal grudge, but when it is used of Allah it is understood free of those associations: His requital springs not from rage but from justice and wisdom.

The name is a reminder that oppression does not go unanswered and that no wronged person's right is ever lost. In the Qur'an the phrase dhu intiqam, "Owner of Retribution," usually appears alongside al-Aziz, the Mighty, pairing power with justice. It is best understood together with the names around it; in the traditional listing it is followed immediately by al-Afuww, the Pardoning.

Surah Ibrahim assures the reader that Allah will never break His promise to His messengers, and the verse closes by describing Him as Exalted in Might and Owner of Retribution. Read in context, the name is less a threat than a guarantee: the promise made to those who walk in truth will be kept.

verses.text: So never think that Allah will fail in His promise to His messengers. Indeed, Allah is Exalted in Might and Owner of Retribution.

81.reflection: When someone wrongs you, the urge to get even can be strong. Al-Muntaqim reminds you that the final word on justice is not yours to carry, and that no right is ever truly lost. This isn't about swallowing your hurt; it's about entrusting it to a just Lord and putting down the weight of resentment. Seeking your due through fair means and choosing to forgive both have a place within that trust. Meanwhile, take care that your own words and actions never infringe on anyone else's rights.
81.practice: Think of one small way you may have wronged someone without meaning to (an unpaid debt, a forgotten promise, something borrowed and never returned) and set it right today.

82.name: Al-Afuww
82.meaning: The Pardoner, who erases sins and leaves no trace of them.
82.description:
Al-Afuww comes from the root ʿ-f-w, which means to erase, to wipe out a trace, and to let go of what is owed. Arabs used it for the wind smoothing away footprints in the sand. Allah's pardon is therefore understood not merely as covering a servant's mistake, but as wiping it away entirely.

This sets al-Afuww subtly apart from al-Ghafur, the Forgiving: forgiveness covers a sin, while pardon removes even its trace. The name al-Afuww appears five times in the Qur'an, most often paired with al-Ghafur or al-Qadir, the All-Powerful.

In Surah An-Nisa, showing or concealing a good deed and pardoning a wrong are linked directly to Allah being Pardoning and Competent. Pardon is presented not as weakness but as strength at its most mature: the One who is able to do anything chooses to forgive.

verses.text: If [instead] you show [some] good or conceal it or pardon an offense - indeed, Allah is ever Pardoning and Competent.

82.reflection: Sometimes you say you have forgiven someone, yet you keep the whole episode filed away in your mind. Al-Afuww invites you to see pardon as a path that leads toward erasing the trace as well. When you remember how much you yourself need Allah's pardon, it becomes easier to be generous with other people's faults. Forgiving doesn't mean approving of what happened; it means refusing to let it run your life today.
82.practice: Choose one small grievance you've been holding against someone and decide never to bring it up again, to them or to anyone else.

83.name: Ar-Ra'uf
83.meaning: The Most Kind, whose tenderness toward His servants is boundless.
83.description:
Ar-Ra'uf comes from the root r-ʾ-f, the source of the word ra'fah. Ra'fah is described as the most delicate and intense form of mercy, a tenderness aimed especially at relieving hardship and shielding someone from harm.

In the Qur'an, Ar-Ra'uf most often appears alongside Ar-Rahim, as ra'ufun rahim, "Kind and Merciful." Scholars have noted that mercy (rahmah) is a broad goodness and grace, while ra'fah is its gentle, protective edge. That Allah does not burden His servants beyond what they can bear is often seen as one expression of this kindness.

Surah Al-Hadid describes Allah sending down clear verses to bring people out of darkness into light, and ties this directly to His being Kind and Merciful toward them. Guidance itself is presented as one of the greatest signs of His tenderness.

verses.text: It is He who sends down upon His Servant [Muhammad (ﷺ)] verses of clear evidence that He may bring you out from darknesses into the light. And indeed, Allah is to you Kind and Merciful.

83.reflection: Kindness often lives less in grand sacrifices than in small, thoughtful gestures. Ar-Ra'uf reminds you that you are surrounded by a tenderness that shields you from burdens you couldn't carry and lights the way ahead. Once you notice that, it becomes easier to be gentle with yourself and with others. Try to see the quiet weight someone near you is carrying today; sometimes a single kind word is enough to change their day.
83.practice: Take one small task off the plate of someone you know is tired or going through a hard time, without waiting to be asked.

84.name: Malik al-Mulk
84.meaning: The true Owner of all dominion and sovereignty.
84.description:
Malik al-Mulk joins two words from the root m-l-k: malik, the one who owns, and mulk, everything that can be owned, along with dominion and rule. Together they mean "Owner of Sovereignty" - the One who owns ownership itself.

The name reaches a step beyond al-Malik, the King. People own things and exercise authority for a while, but all of it is on loan, and its real owner is Allah. Every position, fortune, and opportunity in human hands looks, next to this true ownership, like a temporary trust.

The name appears in the Qur'an in Surah Aal-Imran, verse 26, within a prayer. The verse declares that He gives sovereignty and takes it away, that honor and humiliation are in His hands, and that all good lies in His hand.

verses.text: Say, "O Allah, Owner of Sovereignty, You give sovereignty to whom You will and You take sovereignty away from whom You will. You honor whom You will and You humble whom You will. In Your hand is [all] good. Indeed, You are over all things competent. …

84.reflection: Think of everything you have as something you'll one day hand on: your home, your work, your time, even your talents. Malik al-Mulk puts both the fear of losing and the hunger for more into perspective. When you treat what you've been given as a trust to use well rather than something you're owed, you tend to become both more generous and more at peace. And when something slips out of your hands, knowing who its real Owner is makes the loss lighter.
84.practice: Give something you haven't used in a long time to someone who might actually need it.

85.name: Dhul-Jalali wal-Ikram
85.description:
This name brings two ideas together. Jalal comes from the root j-l-l and conveys greatness, exaltedness, and awe. Ikram comes from k-r-m and means generosity, grace, and hospitality offered without expecting anything back. Dhu simply means "possessor of."

The name expresses that Allah holds both a majesty no mind can encompass and a boundless generosity toward His servants. Majesty suggests distance; generosity suggests closeness. This name says both are united in Him: His awe never overshadows His kindness, and His kindness never diminishes His awe.

The phrase appears twice in Surah Ar-Rahman (verses 27 and 78). Verses 26-27 declare that everything on earth will perish, while the Face of your Lord, Owner of Majesty and Honor, remains.

verses.text: Everyone upon it [i.e., the earth] will perish, And there will remain the Face of your Lord, Owner of Majesty and Honor.

85.reflection: Some moments leave you speechless: a vast landscape, a night full of stars, a baby's first breath. Dhul-Jalali wal-Ikram reminds you that the One behind that grandeur is also the One who is generous to you. Thinking about how everything passes can make you sad, but knowing that what remains is both majestic and generous turns that sadness into trust. The next time you give something, try giving without expecting anything in return.
85.practice: Offer a small treat or kindness to a guest, a coworker, or a family member today for no particular reason.

86.name: Al-Muqsit
86.meaning: The Just, who does everything with equity and puts every right in its place.
86.description:
Al-Muqsit comes from the root q-s-t. Qist means justice and a fair share: keeping the measure full and giving everything its due. Interestingly, qasit, from the same root, describes someone who deviates from what is right, while muqsit describes the one who removes injustice and establishes fairness.

Allah's justice shows not only on the Day of Judgment but in the very balance of creation. He watches over the rights of the wronged and gives everyone their due. The Qur'an asks the same of people: the word muqsitin, "those who act justly," from the same root, is used in several verses to describe those whom Allah loves (for example, Al-Ma'idah 5:42 and Al-Hujurat 49:9).

The name al-Muqsit does not appear in this exact form as a description of Allah in the Qur'an. However, the phrase qa'iman bil-qist in Surah Aal-Imran, verse 18, links justice directly to the testimony of His oneness.

verses.text: Allah witnesses that there is no deity except Him, and [so do] the angels and those of knowledge - [that He is] maintaining [creation] in justice. There is no deity except Him, the Exalted in Might, the Wise.

86.reflection: Justice isn't tested only in courtrooms; it's tested when you listen to the other side of an argument, divide up a task, or settle a dispute between children. Al-Muqsit calls you to measure everyone with the same scale, whether you like them or not. Telling the truth even when it doesn't work in your favor is the hardest and most valuable form of fairness. Today, try asking yourself before each decision: "Is this fair to everyone involved?"
86.practice: Before you settle a disagreement today, restate the other person's point of view in your own words once.

87.name: Al-Jami'
87.meaning: The Gatherer, who brings together what is scattered and gathers humanity on the Day of Judgment.
87.description:
Al-Jami' comes from the root j-m-ʿ, meaning to gather, to bring together, and to unite. Holding seemingly opposite things together in harmony also falls within the meaning of this root.

The name can be understood on several levels. Allah brings the diverse elements of the universe together in order, draws hearts toward one another, and gathers what has been scattered. In its clearest sense, He is the One who will gather all people on a Day about which there is no doubt.

The name appears in Surah Aal-Imran, verse 9, within a prayer, in the sense of "the One who will gather the people." The words that follow, "Allah does not fail in His promise," stress that this gathering is a certain promise.

verses.text: Our Lord, surely You will gather the people for a Day about which there is no doubt. Indeed, Allah does not fail in His promise."

87.reflection: Sometimes the pieces of your life feel scattered: unfinished projects, friendships that drifted, memories that don't seem to connect. Al-Jami' reminds you that what looks scattered can be brought together. You, too, can be someone who brings people together and mends what has come apart. A single small step can be enough to restore a connection that's been broken for years.
87.practice: Call a relative or friend you haven't spoken to in a long time and ask how they're doing.

88.name: Al-Ghaniyy
88.meaning: The Self-Sufficient, free of all need and limitless in wealth.
88.description:
Al-Ghaniyy comes from the root gh-n-y, which conveys wealth, sufficiency, and freedom from need. Allah being al-Ghaniyy means He needs nothing at all, in His being, His attributes, or His actions.

Human wealth is relative and temporary; even someone who has a great deal still needs countless other things. Allah's self-sufficiency is absolute: He needs neither the worship nor the praise of His servants, and the benefit of worship and good deeds returns to the people who do them. In the Qur'an, al-Ghaniyy frequently appears with al-Hamid, the Praiseworthy: He depends on no one, and because His richness is joined with generosity, He is worthy of all praise.

Surah Fatir, verse 15, reminds people that they are in need of Allah while He is Free of need and Praiseworthy. The verse presents human need not as something shameful, but as a reason to turn to the right door.

verses.text: O mankind, you are those in need of Allah, while Allah is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy.

88.reflection: Sometimes the feeling that you don't have enough leaves you restless. Al-Ghaniyy reminds you that true richness belongs to Him, and that your own neediness points you to the right door. Admitting you're in need doesn't make you smaller; it frees you to expect less from people and trust Allah more. Today, try counting what you have instead of what you lack.
88.practice: Skip one purchase today that you were planning to make but don't actually need.

89.name: Al-Mughni
89.meaning: The Enricher, who frees from need and makes sufficient whom He wills.
89.description:
Al-Mughni shares the root gh-n-y with al-Ghaniyy. Al-Ghaniyy is the One who is rich in Himself; al-Mughni is the One who makes others rich and frees them from need. The two names are often reflected on together as a complementary pair.

The enrichment Allah gives is not limited to material means. Freeing the heart from dependence on others, and granting inner richness and contentment, also fall within this name. A well-known hadith of the Prophet states that real wealth is not an abundance of possessions, but richness of the soul.

This meaning appears in Surah An-Najm, verse 48: He is the One who enriches and suffices. In Surah Ad-Duha, the Prophet is reminded that he was found in need and made self-sufficient, a reminder that recognizing past blessings brings confidence for the present.

verses.text: And that it is He who enriches and suffices…
And He found you poor and made [you] self-sufficient.

89.reflection: Look back at an earlier season of your life: what were you lacking then, and what do you have now? Al-Mughni reminds you of the One who made you sufficient when you were in need. That memory offers hope in the face of whatever feels missing today. When you realize that wealth lives not just in your bank account but in contentment and in what you're able to share, you can become a means of meeting someone else's needs too.
89.practice: Quietly meet a small need of someone who is struggling today, without letting them know it came from you.

90.name: Al-Mani'
90.meaning: The Preventer, who withholds as He wills and shields His servants from harm.
90.description:
Al-Mani' comes from the root m-n-ʿ, meaning to prevent, to hold back, and to protect. The name carries a double meaning: it includes both withholding something and guarding someone from it.

Allah's being al-Mani' shows sometimes in not granting a servant something, and sometimes in shielding them from harm. When you don't get what you wanted, it can feel like a loss, yet that very barrier may be protection from a harm you can't see. Giving and withholding are understood together; the Prophet's supplications include the words, "O Allah, none can withhold what You give, and none can give what You withhold."

The name al-Mani' does not appear in this exact form in the Qur'an, but its meaning is clearly expressed in Surah Fatir, verse 2: whatever mercy Allah opens for people, none can withhold, and whatever He withholds, none can release after Him.

verses.text: Whatever Allah grants to people of mercy - none can withhold it; and whatever He withholds - none can release it thereafter. And He is the Exalted in Might, the Wise.

90.reflection: Think of something you wanted badly that never happened. What looked like a disappointment back then may have steered you toward a different door. Al-Mani' reminds you that not every "no" is a loss; sometimes it's protection. Seeing things this way makes it easier to meet obstacles with patience and reflection rather than frustration. You can also choose, now and then, to hold yourself back from habits that do you harm.
90.practice: Set aside one draining habit for just today (for example, scrolling your phone late at night).

91.name: Ad-Darr
91.meaning: The One who, by His wisdom, creates hardship; always understood alongside An-Nafi'.
91.description:
Ad-Darr comes from the root d-r-r, meaning harm, hardship, and constraint. In the lists of the Beautiful Names it always appears side by side with An-Nafi', the Benefactor, and it is understood not on its own but together with it: harm and benefit alike are created by Allah alone.

This paired name teaches that nothing in existence happens outside His will. The hardships people face are not random or meaningless; they unfold within a measure and a wisdom. Scholars have pointed out that difficulty may be a test, a wake-up call, a path to maturity, or the means to a greater good.

Ad-Darr does not appear in this exact form in the Qur'an, but its meaning is expressed in Surah Yunus, verse 107: if Allah touches you with adversity, none can remove it but Him, and if He intends good for you, none can repel His bounty. That the verse closes with "He is the Forgiving, the Merciful" shows that this name must be understood alongside mercy and forgiveness.

verses.text: And if Allah should touch you with adversity, there is no remover of it except Him; and if He intends for you good, then there is no repeller of His bounty. He causes it to reach whom He wills of His servants. And He is the Forgiving, the Merciful.

91.reflection: When you're going through a hard season, the question "Why me?" can take over your thoughts. Ad-Darr reminds you that even this difficulty falls within a measure and a wisdom, and that He is also the One who can lift it. This doesn't mean minimizing the pain; it means carrying it with trust rather than a sense of meaninglessness. Sharing your burden, asking for help, and doing what you reasonably can are all part of that trust. Knowing that harm and benefit come from the same Hand keeps hope alive even when every door seems shut.
91.practice: Set aside time today to simply listen to someone going through a hard time, without offering solutions.

92.name: An-Nafi'
92.meaning: The Benefactor, who creates all benefit and good.
92.description:
An-Nafi' comes from the root n-f-ʿ, meaning benefit, usefulness, and advantage. It forms a pair with Ad-Darr and is understood together with it: Allah alone creates both benefit and harm, and nothing can be of benefit without His permission.

When a piece of knowledge, a word, a friendship, or an effort does someone good, it happens, beyond all the visible causes, by His will. People take the means and put in the work, but they hope in Allah for the outcome to turn out well. This name also reminds us that people are called to be of benefit to one another.

An-Nafi' does not appear in this exact form in the Qur'an, but its meaning is expressed in Surah Al-An'am, verse 17: if Allah touches you with adversity, none can remove it but Him, and if He touches you with good, He is over all things competent. The Qur'an also points out in many places how pointless it is to turn, instead of Allah, to things that hold no power of harm or benefit.

verses.text: And if Allah should touch you with adversity, there is no remover of it except Him. And if He touches you with good - then He is over all things competent.

92.reflection: Try to notice the good that reaches you today: something you learned, help you received, a word that came at just the right moment. An-Nafi' points you to the real source of these benefits and turns you toward gratitude. At the same time, you can be a channel through which that good reaches others. You don't need great resources to be useful; sharing what you know or making someone's task a little easier is benefit too.
92.practice: Teach someone who could use it a piece of knowledge or a skill that you think would help them.

93.name: An-Nur
93.meaning: The Light of the heavens and the earth, who illuminates and makes all things visible.
93.description:
An-Nur comes from the root n-w-r, meaning light, brightness, and radiance. Light is that which is visible in itself and makes other things visible. Allah being An-Nur is understood as His bringing beings out of the darkness of nonexistence into being, and giving people a light by which they can see the truth.

Scholars have explained this name without limiting it to physical light: Allah is the illuminator of the heavens and the earth, the One who gives knowledge to minds and guidance to hearts. The Qur'an often speaks of revelation, faith, and guidance as "light," and the phrase "bringing out of darkness into light" recurs in many verses.

The name appears directly in verse 35 of the surah that bears it, Surah An-Nur: "Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth." The verse describes this light through the parable of a lamp, a glass, and a clear olive oil, and deepens it with the words "light upon light."

verses.text: Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth. The example of His light is like a niche within which is a lamp; the lamp is within glass, the glass as if it were a pearly [white] star lit from [the oil of] a blessed olive tree, neither of the east nor of the west, whose oil would almost glow even if untouched by fire. Light upon light. Allah guides to His light whom He wills. And Allah presents examples for the people, and Allah is Knowing of all things.

93.reflection: In a dark room, even one small candle changes everything. An-Nur reminds you that light is possible even in the corners of your life that feel darkest. If something has you confused, slowing down to think, learning more, and seeking advice are the doors that open onto that light. You can be a lamp for the people around you, too: through a good word, honest advice, or a hopeful attitude.
93.practice: Talk through something that's been confusing you with someone whose knowledge and honesty you trust.

94.name: Al-Hadi
94.meaning: The Guide, who shows the right path and leads to it.
94.description:
Al-Hadi comes from the root h-d-y, meaning to show the way, to lead to the right path, and to guide. The word hidayah, guidance, shares this root. It covers both pointing out the way and helping someone walk it.

Allah's guidance can be understood on several levels: inspiring every living thing with what it needs to live, giving people reason and conscience, making the way clear through prophets and scriptures, and turning hearts toward walking that way. In Surah Ta-Ha, Moses describes his Lord as the One who gave each thing its form and then guided it.

The name appears in Surah Al-Furqan, verse 31: "sufficient is your Lord as a guide and a helper." The verse acknowledges that every prophet faced opposition, and emphasizes that for anyone walking the right path, Allah is enough as guide and helper.

verses.text: And thus have We made for every prophet an enemy from among the criminals. But sufficient is your Lord as a guide and a helper.

94.reflection: There are moments when two roads lie ahead and you can't tell which one is right. Al-Hadi reminds you that a heart asking for direction is not left alone. Guidance isn't a one-time event; it's a path you ask for and walk again every day. When you guide others, you can choose to do it without judgment, with patience, and by example.
94.practice: Help a new coworker, a new neighbor, or someone who's lost find their way in a way that genuinely makes things easier for them.

95.name: Al-Badi'
95.meaning: The Originator, who creates without any prior model.
95.description:
Al-Badi' comes from the root b-d-ʿ, meaning to bring something into being for the first time, with nothing like it before. Al-Badi' is both the One who creates without precedent and the One whose creations carry a matchless beauty.

Human creativity is really a rearranging of materials that already exist; Allah's creation needs no example, material, or model. The fact that every face, every fingerprint, and every leaf is different from every other can be seen as a visible trace of this name.

The name appears twice in the Qur'an as Badi' as-samawati wal-ard, "Originator of the heavens and the earth" (Al-Baqarah 2:117 and Al-An'am 6:101). The verse in Al-Baqarah adds that when He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is.

verses.text: Originator of the heavens and the earth. When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is.

95.reflection: Today, try looking at the world around you not out of habit but as if seeing it for the first time: the veins of a leaf, the shape of the clouds, the face of someone you love. Al-Badi' reminds you that everything was made with unmatched artistry, and that you are part of that uniqueness. Instead of comparing yourself to others, focus on the particular gifts you've been given. Bringing care and beauty into your own work is one way of living this name.
95.practice: Spend five minutes looking closely at a tree or a flower outside and find one detail you've never noticed before.

96.name: Al-Baqi
96.meaning: The Everlasting, whose existence has no end and who remains after all else perishes.
96.description:
Al-Baqi comes from the root b-q-y, meaning to remain, to continue, and to endure. Allah being al-Baqi means His existence has no end; it depends on nothing else and will never cease.

The name is closely related to al-Awwal and al-Akhir, the First and the Last. Everything we see in the universe has a beginning and an end: seasons change, people come and go, works wear out. Al-Baqi points to what stays unchanged in the midst of all this change. The Qur'an also gives the good news that the good people do will endure with Allah.

Surah An-Nahl, verse 96, says: "Whatever you have will end, but what Allah has is lasting." Surah Ar-Rahman, verse 27, likewise declares that everything on earth will perish, and only the Face of your Lord will remain.

verses.text: Whatever you have will end, but what Allah has is lasting. And We will surely give those who were patient their reward according to the best of what they used to do.

96.reflection: It can hurt to think that something you've poured yourself into will one day wear out or disappear. Al-Baqi reminds you that true permanence lies with Him and in what is with Him. That awareness keeps you from clinging too tightly to what is passing, while assuring you that the good you do is never wasted. Today, you might make time for one small kindness that will leave a lasting mark.
96.practice: Do one small good deed today whose benefit will outlast you, such as donating a book you've read to a library or to someone who will read it.

97.name: Al-Warith
97.meaning: The Inheritor, to whom everything returns when all else has passed away.
97.description:
Al-Warith comes from the root w-r-th, meaning inheritance, to inherit, and to come into possession of what someone leaves behind. Allah being al-Warith means that when all beings have passed away, everything will remain His alone.

People use what they own for a time and then leave it behind; inheritance passes from one generation to the next. But at the end of all this changing of hands, everything returns to its true Owner. Reflected on together with al-Baqi and Malik al-Mulk, this name deepens the realization that whatever is in our hands is a trust.

In Surah Al-Hijr, verse 23, Allah declares that it is He who gives life and causes death, and that He is the Inheritor. In Surah Al-Anbiya, verse 89, Zechariah turns to his Lord saying, "You are the best of inheritors," a prayer that shows, even in the midst of longing for a child, where his deepest trust lay.

verses.text: And indeed, it is We who give life and cause death, and We are the Inheritor.
And [mention] Zechariah, when he called to his Lord, "My Lord, do not leave me alone [with no heir], while You are the best of inheritors."

97.reflection: Have you ever thought about what you'll leave behind? Al-Warith reminds you that possessions will one day change hands, but good character, a true word, and meaningful work leave a lasting trace. In moments when you feel alone, you can turn, as Zechariah did, to the One who will never leave you by yourself. Think today about how the traces you leave might echo in other people's lives tomorrow.
97.practice: Share a life lesson that matters to you with a younger family member or friend today.

98.name: Ar-Rashid
98.meaning: The Rightly Guiding, whose every act is sound and who leads His servants to maturity.
98.description:
Ar-Rashid comes from the root r-sh-d, which conveys finding the right way, maturity, sound judgment, and wise decision-making. The related word rushd refers to reaching the maturity needed to manage one's own affairs. Rashid means both one who is on the right path and one who directs others to it.

Allah being Ar-Rashid is understood in two ways: first, that all His acts and decrees are perfectly sound and wise; second, that He shows His servants what is right and leads them toward maturity. The name is closely related to al-Hadi, but rushd goes beyond knowing the way to include walking it with good judgment.

The name Ar-Rashid does not appear in this exact form as a description of Allah in the Qur'an. However, the word rashad, from the same root, appears in the prayer of the youths who took refuge in the cave in Surah Al-Kahf, verse 10. Their prayer is a beautiful example of asking Allah for right direction in a difficult situation.

verses.text: [Mention] when the youths retreated to the cave and said, "Our Lord, grant us from Yourself mercy and prepare for us from our affair right guidance."

98.reflection: On the edge of an important decision, it's easy to rush. Ar-Rashid reminds you that a sound decision takes both careful reasoning and asking Allah for what is right. Like the youths of the cave, praying "make the right way easy for me" in an uncertain moment isn't a substitute for thinking; it's trust placed alongside it. Maturity doesn't mean never making mistakes; it means learning from them and turning toward what is better.
98.practice: Write down the pros and cons of a decision you've been putting off.

99.name: As-Sabur
99.meaning: The Most Patient, who does not hasten punishment and leaves all things to their appointed time.
99.description:
As-Sabur comes from the root s-b-r, meaning to restrain oneself, to endure, and to wait. The form sabur signals that this quality is abundant and constant. Applied to Allah, patience does not mean enduring hardship; it means not hastening to punish His servants for their mistakes and leaving everything to the time He has decreed.

The name is close in meaning to al-Halim, the Forbearing; both describe Allah's unhurried gentleness toward His servants. As-Sabur especially highlights that everything is left to an appointed time. That delay is itself a mercy, giving people the chance to turn back and set things right.

As-Sabur does not appear in this exact form as a description of Allah in the Qur'an, but its meaning is clear in Surah An-Nahl, verse 61: if Allah were to hold people immediately to account for their wrongdoing, He would not leave a single creature on earth, yet He defers them for a specified term. The Qur'an also encourages patience in people, with the good news that "Allah is with the patient" (Al-Baqarah 2:153). In the traditional listing, it is the last of the Beautiful Names.

verses.text: And if Allah were to impose blame on the people for their wrongdoing, He would not have left upon it [i.e., the earth] any creature, but He defers them for a specified term. And when their term has come, they will not remain behind an hour, nor will they precede [it].

99.reflection: Wanting things to happen right away is part of being human: a result, an answer, a change. As-Sabur reminds you how patient Allah is with His servants, giving them time to return. When you notice the patience shown to you, it becomes easier to be understanding about how slowly other people change. Patience isn't passive waiting; it's continuing to do what is right while leaving the outcome to its time. Show yourself a little patience today, too.
99.practice: The next time something makes you impatient today, take one deep breath and pause for a few seconds before you respond.
